Monday's meeting will be chaired by the Turkish foreign and defence ministers as well as the chief of the general staff.
Pakistan is sending Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, along with the defence minister and the commander of the defence forces.
Saudi Arabia will be represented by its foreign minister, the defence minister and the chief of the general staff, Turkish sources said.
As well as international security, the participants plan to address boosting defence capabilities, the interoperability of their armed forces, and their cooperation in the defence industry, Ankara said.
The Israeli strike in Gaza's Deir al-Balah earlier this morning killed a three-year-old child and a man, according to local health officials.
Medics said the Israeli airstrike near a bakery killed one man, Hussam Nusair, a three-year-old boy, Tayyem Hamdan, and wounded several others.
Israel has killed at least five Palestinians in Gaza over the past 24 hours, according to Gaza's health ministry.
At least 1,318 people have been killed by Israeli forces since the "ceasefire" was supposed to come into effect in October, the ministry said in its daily bulletin.
The Israeli army has carried out a "massive" explosion in the border town of Houla in Lebanon's Marjayoun district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.
Israel's far-right national security minister on Sunday boasted of worsening conditions for Palestinian prisoners as he visited female inmates.
Two months before elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir posted a video in which a veiled woman, her face blurred out, said that prisoners had "extremely bad" conditions and "don't get any rights, and we have particular needs as women".
"We haven't bathed for three days and we haven't changed our underwear," she said, warning of the risk of disease.
Ben-Gvir responds approvingly as he compares the treatment to that of captives held for up to two years by Hamas and other fighters in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 attack.
"Our hostages had no shampoo and had no such conditions. I am proud that we have succeeded in reducing the terrorists' prison conditions to the bare minimum. The summer camps in the prisons are over," Ben Gvir said.
Militant settlers are continuing to rampage in the occupied West Bank as pogroms against Palestinians intensify across the territory. Attacks against Palestinian civilians were reported in a dozen locations on Sunday, including in villages near Nablus and Ramallah, Masafer Yatta and Al-Mughayyir.
Hundreds of settlers raided Islamic religious sites in the village of Awarta, southeast of Nablus, under the protection of Israeli forces.
Meanwhile, Israeli soldiers began destroying Palestinian-owned land in the town of Deir Ballut, in the central West Bank.

articles.title: Missile strike hits Belgorod, reportedly damaging Ozon facility and power plant
articles.body:
Smoke rises over Belgorod, Russia, following a reported missile strike on Aug. 30, 2026. (Exilenova+ / Telegram)
Russia's Belgorod came under a missile attack on Aug. 30, with a logistics facility housing an Ozon sorting center and delivery hub damaged in the strike, according to Russian officials and the company.
The attack comes as Ukraine continues targeting Russian military and logistics infrastructure that supports Moscow's war effort.
Acting Belgorod Oblast Governor Alexander Shuvaev said there were casualties and several fires following what he described as a Ukrainian attack. He did not specify the locations of the strikes or provide further details on the number of people injured.
Ozon confirmed that its sorting center and delivery hub in Belgorod had been hit.
A fire broke out at the facility but was later contained, Ozon said. The company suspended deliveries and the acceptance of customer orders and goods from sellers in Belgorod and the surrounding region while it reorganizes its logistics routes.
OSINT Telegram channel Exilenova reported that the attack also damaged the Belgorod thermal power plant. It also reported a strike near the city's television tower.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claims.
Anna Fratsyvir is an assistant opinion editor at the Kyiv Independent, with a background in broadcast journalism and international affairs. Previously, she worked as a news editor at the Kyiv Independent, and as a TV journalist at Ukraine’s public broadcaster Suspilne, covering global politics and international developments. Anna holds a Bachelor's degree in International Communications from Taras Shevchenko National University and is currently an MA candidate in International Relations at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS).
Russian independent media outlet Mediazona, in collaboration with the BBC Russian service, has confirmed the identities of 242,747 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine.
The president's latest report comes amid an ongoing Russian drone attack on the capital with explosions heard in central Kyiv beginning around 12:30 a.m. local time overnight on Aug. 31, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Drones have been flying toward the capital for hours at a time, with explosions and the sound of air defense fire rocking the city throughout the morning and afternoon.
Mykhailo Fedorov said he is seeking backing from venture capitalists, private investors, and U.S. technology companies for a fund that would invest in Ukrainian defense startups and create new companies focused on battlefield technologies.
The company said it is currently assessing the full scale of the consequences and taking steps to restore supplies of its products to customers and consumers in Ukraine.
"Such a meeting is possible only to formalize agreements," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters. He added that a settlement over Ukraine is "not a primitive deal," but a "very complicated" process involving "a huge number of details."
Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert "Madyar" Brovdi said Ukrainian drones targeted the Yeysk airfield in Russia's Krasnodar Krai and the Millerovo airfield in Rostov Oblast.
In Donetsk Oblast, two people were killed, including a 13-year-old child, and two more were injured after Russian forces dropped bombs on houses in the village of Bilbasivka on Aug. 30,
As Russia scales up production of its jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5 — Ukraine is struggling to shoot them down amid prolonged waves of attacks.
Amid intensifying attacks in the Black Sea from both Ukraine and Russia, a Turkish-operated vessel was hit on Aug. 26 off the coast of Tuapse — a Russian port city with a large oil refinery that Ukraine frequently attacks with drones.
Russia launched nearly 2,000 attack drones, more than 1,600 glide bombs, and 31 missiles, including North Korean ballistic missiles, against Ukraine in just the last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on his Telegram channel on Aug. 30.

articles.title: Russia’s Plan to Capture Donbas by March 2027 Is Unrealistic, Says Ukrainian Presidential Official
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Plan to Capture Donbas by March 2027 Is Unrealistic, Says Ukrainian Presidential Official
Russia’s goal is to take full control of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions by the end of 2026. Russia’s military leadership reportedly considers that deadline unrealistic and is asking for more time. Ukraine’s Deputy Head of the Office of the President Pavlo Palisa says that even Moscow’s extended timeline for capturing the regions have little to do with battlefield reality.
Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine Pavlo Palisa met with journalists in Kyiv to discuss the situation on the front and explain how the fighting is developing today. A UNITED24 Media editor attended the meeting and reported the key takeaways.
What is happening on Ukrainian front lines
There is an ongoing trend toward a slowdown in Russia’s rate of advance, says Palisa. On some sectors of the front, there are grounds for “limited optimism,” while units of Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces have been conducting active operations in the Oleksandrivka sector for an extended period.
Moscow’s immediate objective is the Donetsk region. The Kremlin wants it captured by December 31, 2026, while Russia’s military leadership is asking for an additional three months, describing March 31, 2027, as a more realistic deadline.
“My subjective opinion is that even by March 31, this is an unrealistic scenario,” he said.
Here, Palisa’s assessment corresponds with what is happening on the battlefield: Russian forces have made minimal gains in Donetsk region, while their spring-summer campaign can be described as a failure.
At the same time, plans remain in place to establish a buffer zone in the Kharkiv and Sumy regions, and partially in Chernihiv region, to a depth of up to 20 kilometers, with the possibility of expanding it further. This is connected to the increasing depth of the drone “kill zone.”
The Kremlin is also planning for a potential offensive toward Kyiv and Chernihiv.
“I want to emphasize: planning and preparing,” said Palisa. “Several options were indeed being considered. We did receive intelligence to that effect, verified by several sources.”
At the same time, there are currently no signs that Russia is forming an offensive grouping in these directions.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has already developed the corresponding defensive measures.
Mobilization in Russia
In July, verified Russian losses—killed and wounded—amounted to 43,000 personnel, compared with 37,000 newly recruited troops. That is a difference of 6,000 in a single month, Palisa says.
This trend of Russia operating at a manpower “deficit” has continued at least since February of this year, contributing to the situation now seen on the battlefield, Palisa says. Russia is no longer able to compensate for heavy losses through recruitment in the way it did in previous years.
“If we consider the objectives Russia’s political leadership has set for its Armed Forces,” he said, referring to Russia’s plans regarding capturing Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
“Then with the forces currently available and the present rate of recruitment and manpower replenishment, it is obvious both to them and to us that they are incapable of achieving their strategic objectives.”
The figures previously announced remain relevant, he said: 300,000 people are expected to be mobilized this year and another 300,000 during the first half of next year. The Kremlin has reportedly been leaning toward this option since the beginning of the year.
However, conscription is only one challenge. These people must then be clothed, equipped, educated and trained in basic military skills, all of which will require substantial resources. Therefore, a sudden influx of large numbers of Russian troops onto the battlefield should not be expected.
In Palisa’s assessment, these forces will ultimately be sent to Ukraine to fight there. Military provocations against the Baltic states, Poland, or other NATO countries are unlikely, given the difficulties Russia already faces in waging its war against Ukraine, where it has been unable to achieve significant results.
Ukraine’s strikes on Russian territory
A war of this scale requires enormous financial resources from Russia.
“And we are trying to deprive the Russians of the ability to earn that money,” Palisa explained.
This is the primary reason behind Ukraine’s long-range strikes against military targets on Russian territory, and their number is expected to increase.
“The population of the Russian Federation is now feeling their effects,” said Palisa. “We are demonstrating successes, primarily in our ability to apply pressure to vulnerable points and centers of gravity, according to certain priorities and a certain logic. This is gradually producing a cumulative effect and is intended to deliver the result our country needs.
We are developing these capabilities during the war, under extremely difficult conditions—although, of course, with extraordinary support from our partners. We are capable of shifting the war to a certain extent into a new phase.
First and foremost, this concerns strikes against targets that, from a military perspective, do not produce an immediate effect but strategically have a major and long-lasting impact on the enemy.”
This includes strikes against infrastructure affecting energy exports, which account for a significant portion of Russia’s budget; strikes against vessels belonging to the shadow fleet; and attacks on the Russian logistics infrastructure, as well as networks and facilities that enable the functioning of Russia’s logistics system. Such strikes produce both primary and secondary effects.
The challenge of jet-powered drones
Russian forces have significantly increased their use of jet-powered UAVs. Their numbers are expected to continue growing because Russia sees them as effective, says Palisa.
Kyiv experienced the threat firsthand on August 27, when air-raid alerts sounded 13 times in a single day, lasting a combined 15 hours.
“Offensive capabilities always stay ahead of defensive capabilities. We will undoubtedly have to adapt. That will take time,” Palisa said.
He added that the interceptor drones Ukraine currently possesses, which could theoretically intercept jet-powered drones, have so far failed to demonstrate the expected level of effectiveness. Manufacturers, however, are working to address the problem.
By contrast, man-portable air-defense systems, various systems deployed for point air defense, and combat aircraft have demonstrated significant effectiveness.
Ukraine is therefore calling on its partners to provide more air-defense systems to protect its cities.

articles.title: Media suggests what CIA chief discussed during Moscow visit
articles.body:
CIA chief proposed trilateral talks during Moscow visit – Axios
CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed a trilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky during his covert trip to Moscow in an effort to find a resolution to the ongoing Ukraine conflict, Axios has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Ratcliffe made an unannounced trip to Moscow on August 25. The following day, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that contact between the two countries’ intelligence services had taken place, but said Putin had not met with the CIA chief. “Of course, President Putin is immediately briefed on everything,” Peskov said, calling the meeting “a positive phenomenon” while declining to give further details.
Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) chief Sergei Naryshkin later confirmed that he had met with Ratcliffe in Moscow. Naryshkin said the issues discussed were related to the intelligence services. Axios reported that Ratcliffe also met with Federal Security Service (FSB) Director Alexander Bortnikov.
US officials briefed Zelensky on the Moscow talks and the plan for a trilateral summit. They also said Ratcliffe had discussed the possibility of restarting peace talks, the outlet reported.
Earlier last week, Trump described the visit as “semi-routine.” When asked by talk show host Glenn Beck whether Putin planned on “testing NATO resolve,” or whether Ratcliffe discussed US sanctions on Iran, Trump replied “none of the above.”
Ratcliffe’s visit was the first known trip to Moscow by a CIA director since William Burns traveled there in November 2021. The last known face-to-face meeting between the CIA and SVR chiefs was in Ankara in November 2022, when Burns met Naryshkin to discuss nuclear escalation risks and detained US citizens.
The last publicly disclosed contact between Ratcliffe and a senior Russian official was a March 2025 phone call with SVR chief Sergey Naryshkin. The two sides agreed to maintain dialogue to “promote international stability and security” and reduce tensions between Moscow and Washington, the SVR said.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1649: Russia keeps Kyiv under fire for a fourth day as Ukraine tests new interceptors and strikes back at Russian oil
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine is testing four new drone interceptors as Russia floods its skies with faster Gerans. Kyiv is racing to scale new defences after Russia used more than 2,500 jet-powered drones in August alone.
Ukraine strikes Russia's second-largest oil refinery again in major overnight attack, also hitting airfield and drone launch site. The refinery has been targeted repeatedly during the full-scale war as Ukraine strikes infrastructure supporting Russia's military and economy.
Four days of Russian attacks keep Kyiv under near-constant fire. Ukraine is struggling to defend its skies. Russia has launched nearly 2,000 attack drones, more than 1,600 guided bombs and 31 missiles against Ukraine this week, while Kyiv faces repeated strikes and a shortage of critical air defence interceptors.
Ukrainian ground-robot maker has moved into air: Ratel's first strike drone flies 30 kilometres on Starlink link. The Ratel K1 carries two kilograms, the maker says.
"We have surprises for our neighbors": Ukraine's aviation commander says new aircraft developments are essentially finished and already in testing. Ukraine has already rebuilt what it flies. Its crews turned the 1970s-era Su-24 bomber into a launcher for SCALP cruise missiles.
Russia launches third attack on Ukraine's largest Danube port this month, during peak of wheat harvest. Five trucks loaded with grain were destroyed and three more damaged in the Izmail district.
Ukraine chooses three Western fighters to build its air force around. One of them can fly again from stretch of road in 15 to 20 minutes. The Air Force settled on them after weighing cost, logistics, and repair speed.
Fix for Ukraine's interceptors is radar seeker head, and American firm is selling one for $4,000, says president's tech adviser. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov says cloud and fog collapse interceptor hit rates, and a seeker head is the way out.
Four ground robots for one evacuation: Russia is targeting Ukraine's robotic medevac missions. Ground robots are helping evacuate wounded troops from exposed positions, but the systems themselves have come under intense Russian fire.
Ukrainian robot commander calls ground robots "Persian elephants." What army really needs are "Arabian steeds," he says. A "Khartia" robot commander says FPV drones and mines have collapsed the machines' lifespan.
Russia destroyed last of Kherson's heat and power equipment on 26 August. Ukraine's new defence minister arrived days later. Yevhenii Khmara met the regional governor days after glide bombs wrecked the city's power plant.
Ukraine has built twin-Kalashnikov turret for cheap ground robots. Security Service has already used one to destroy Russian ambushes. A Brave1 turret carries two AKs and went from idea to prototype in under six months.
Ukraine struck Tu-95 at base Russia launches its cruise missiles on Ukraine's civilians. Satellite image shows third of right wing gone. SBU Alpha struck the strategic bomber at Engels-2.
Kyiv has been under attack for 2 days nonstop. Russia is targeting the capital's civilian supply chains. Russian jet-powered drones have repeatedly struck warehouses, businesses and logistics facilities around the capital, disrupting supplies while rescuers work under threat of further attacks.
Intelligence and technology
Ukraine's intelligence: Russia is running its Nepal, Cuba, Kenya, and India recruitment scheme in Indonesia now. Ukraine's foreign intelligence says it holds documents on at least eight recruited Indonesian citizens.
Partisans say Russian recruiters in occupied Donetsk are taking drunk men from bars straight to enlistment offices. An ATESH agent inside the Dnepr grouping headquarters reports a new scheme.
Russians bought $300 million in body armor, thermal sights, and drone parts on Ozon marketplace Ukraine is bombing. Russians bought 157,700 body armour vests there.
International
After CIA head's visit to Moscow, Poland's PM warns Russia is preparing to escalate war. He puts critical window at seven or eight months. Poland's prime minister says there are signals of serious Russian preparation.
Ukraine dismissed its defence minister in July. He is now advising NATO country on defence innovation. Guido Crozetto called the dismissed Ukrainian minister the day after Kyiv let him go.
From the Gripen sale to coast guard boats: Sweden sends 10 vessels to Ukraine. Ukraine's emergency service will use the boats for waterborne rescue work, including clearing mines from river beds. Stockholm's contributions to the US-led PURL programme now total $552 million.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russia has burned millions of Ukrainian books, striking at the infrastructure of Ukrainian culture. More than 60,000 books were destroyed in a single warehouse strike near Kyiv this week, adding to losses that publishers say are becoming impossible to absorb.
Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine's modern commercial storage capacity. Retail logistics are being reshaped. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi says the country faces no threat of famine, but warns stores could see a narrower range of products.
Political and legal developments
What does Ukraine's new defence minister wear on his wrist? He did not mention it until reporter asked. Yevhenii Khmara's bracelet carries the names of fallen comrades, a US magazine reported.
"Territory that will allow us to export our energy resources to Europe": Russia's deputy Duma chairman calls for massed bombing of Ukrainian cities. Duma vice-speaker Pyotr Tolstoy said the aim is to demoralise civilians until they give up.

articles.title: ‘It makes no sense’ for Moscow to attack NATO – Finland’s president
articles.body:
‘It makes no sense’ for Moscow to attack NATO – Finland’s president
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has said that he doesn’t believe speculations that Russia is planning to attack NATO countries.
Russia has repeatedly rejected claims that it has aggressive designs against the bloc, saying that they are only made by Western politicians to distract the public from problems at home and justify growing military spending.
During his interview with the German tabloid Bild on Saturday, Stubb was asked to weigh in on the assessment by the Defense Ministry in Berlin that Russia could invade NATO territory by 2029.
“If someone had such a crystal ball – wonderful. But I just don’t see any evidence or facts for it,” he replied.
“First, I have intelligence findings. And secondly, we have a deterrence – and this deterrence is stronger than that of any other military power anywhere in the world,” the Finnish president added.
Given NATO’s conventional forces, missile arsenals and nuclear weapons stockpiles, “it does not make sense for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance,” he said.
According to Stubb, Russia is also preoccupied with the Ukraine conflict.
“I simply don’t see that they could now suddenly mobilize forces for two fronts,” he noted.
“I’m not saying: ‘Relax.’ You should always prepare for the worst to prevent it,” the Finnish president said.
He accused Moscow of waging “information warfare” against the West, saying that “Russia wants us Europeans to sit here and discuss: Will Russia escalate?.. Will Russia attack NATO and Europe?”
Stubb again urged NATO to continue its support for Kiev amid the ongoing conflict with Moscow. Finland joined the bloc in 2023, abandoning its longstanding policy of neutrality.
“We have to understand, you in Germany and we in Finland, that Ukraine is the best security guarantee we have against Russia. If Ukraine loses, we lose,” he argued.
Moscow maintains that a conflict with NATO is only possible if the bloc launches an aggression against Russia first.
Earlier this week, Moscow told the UK that its military facilities and equipment in Ukraine and beyond could become legitimate targets for Russia if Kiev continues to use British-supplied weapons for strikes on Russian territory.
Russian officials also previously warned that if Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania knowingly help to facilitate Ukrainian drone attacks against northwestern Russia, Moscow could consider them complicit in those actions and would have the right to self-defense under the UN Charter.

articles.title: Finland says it ‘makes no sense’ for Russia to risk attack on a Nato nation
articles.body:
Finland says it ‘makes no sense’ for Russia to risk attack on a Nato nation
President Stubb said he did not believe Moscow was in a position to go to war with the military alliance
Finland’s President Alexander Stubb said he did not believe Russia would risk an attack against a Nato country, telling Germany’s Bild newspaper it would “make no sense” to test the resolve of the alliance.
Western officials have warned of a growing risk of Russian hybrid operations, including cyberattacks, against European countries potentially leading to a direct confrontation with the Nato alliance. German officials have said they assess Russia would be in a position to attack a Nato country by 2029.
“If anyone has a crystal ball like that – that’s great. I simply see neither evidence nor facts to support it,” he told Bild in an interview published on Saturday, adding he did not believe that Russia “would ever want to attack Nato, the world’s most powerful military alliance”.
Stubb, whose country joined Nato in 2023, abandoning its previous policy of neutrality following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine a year earlier, said the alliance had to be prepared for any scenario but he did not believe Moscow was in a position to go to war with Nato.
He said Nato’s strength in conventional weapons, missiles and nuclear weapons was too strong to attack, adding that he had intelligence information to back his assessment.

articles.title: US Strike On Iranian Launchers Signals Resolve To Keep Hormuz Open, Experts Say
articles.body:
WASHINGTON -- US forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz after the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) was observed preparing to launch rockets carrying sea mines into the vital waterway, a US official confirmed to RFE/RL.
The August 30 strikes mark the first publicly reported direct US attack on Iranian military positions in more than a month and come as Washington seeks to restore shipping through one of the world's most strategically important maritime chokepoints.
The US official said the IRGC forces were preparing to launch the rockets with sea mines into the strait. Last week, US Central Command said American forces had completed clearing sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes and were keeping a close watch on activity there.
“US forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway,” the official said.
US Central Command said that "US forces took limited, precise action against IRGC mine-laying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz. In essence, Iran created the threat and the US military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce."
Iran's hard-line IRGC vowed retaliation. In a statement carried by Iranian state media, it acknowledged “the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots” and said the attack would “result in the punishment of the aggressor.”
The IRGC later said it fired ballistic missiles at two bases housing US forces in Jordan in retaliation. Jordan, a close US ally, said it intercepted eight incoming missiles that entered its airspace early on August 31.
A Warning Over Hormuz
Experts interviewed by RFE/RL said the US strike is less significant as an isolated military action than as a demonstration that Washington is prepared to use force to prevent Iran from restoring its ability to threaten shipping through Hormuz.
Alex Plitsas, a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council and a former Pentagon official, said the latest exchange began after Iran struck a ship off the coast of Oman.
“Today’s tit-for-tat strikes began after Iran struck a ship off the coast of Oman and then was attempting to launch a small number of mines into the strait,” Plitsas told RFE/RL. “The US struck the launchers.”
Plitsas said he believed Iran's attack on the ship was “in direct response to US statements about increased oil flows out of the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks,” intended to demonstrate that Tehran could still strike maritime targets and increase the risk level for shippers.
The distinction between a physically blocked waterway and a waterway made too dangerous for commercial traffic is crucial, he said.
“The strait itself is physically open,” Plitsas said. “Reduced flow at this point is largely due to the risk of an Iranian attack on a ship.”
That means clearing mines and destroying identified launch sites may not be enough to restore normal traffic. Iran can continue using missiles and drones to threaten vessels, and the US cannot eliminate every potential launch site or weapon.
“It’ll be virtually impossible to strike every Iranian missile or drone, so the Iranians can continue to harass ships and keep the strait held at risk for some time,” Plitsas said.
He said the current situation could persist in the absence of a return to large-scale combat, until pressure on Iran produces a negotiated settlement.
The result is a difficult test for Washington. The military objective is to protect the waterway, but commercial operators must also be convinced that the risk of sailing through Hormuz has fallen enough to justify resuming regular traffic.
Not A New Phase Of War
Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran, said the strike was a signal that Washington would not allow Iran to reverse what he described as American gains in recent weeks in ensuring freedom of navigation in Hormuz.
“I think today’s strike is a signal from the US that it is not going to allow Iran to reverse the American gains in recent weeks over ensuring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz,” Brodsky told RFE/RL.
But Brodsky cautioned against portraying the attack as the beginning of an entirely new phase of the conflict.
“It’s not a decisive shift to a new phase of the war,” he said. “Rather it is a reminder that the US has the will to police the Strait of Hormuz.”
The more consequential development may be Iran's response. Speaking before the report of the IRGC's retaliatory strikes, Brodsky said Tehran is expected to lash out as it suffers economically, and that US policymakers understand the dynamic.
“How the US responds to any Iranian attacks will matter most,” he said. A decisive American response will be required to demonstrate that the US has the endurance to continue the blockade for as long as Iran refuses to submit to US demands.”
That could create a cycle in which Iran seeks to impose costs on US forces or shipping without returning to full-scale war, while Washington responds whenever it determines that Iranian actions threaten navigation.
Hormuz Open, But Traffic Severely Constrained
Ian Ralby, head of the maritime-security firm Auxilium Worldwide, said the US strike underscores that the conflict between the US and Iran remains unresolved.
“I think today’s strike indicates what any serious observer has known all along -- which is there remains an international armed conflict between the US and Iran,” Ralby told RFE/RL. He said the attack showed that there are “a number of unresolved issues that do not have any clear timeline for their resolution.”
The continued weakness of shipping through Hormuz illustrates the problem. Ralby said traffic is among the lowest seen during the conflict, with about five vessels a day traveling in either direction and some days with no traffic at all.
For Ralby, that demonstrates that Washington remains “poised and ready and willing to use force against Iran -- both at sea and in its sovereign territory -- in order to accomplish its goals.”
But military action alone cannot remove the risks facing commercial operators. Even an attack that does not close the waterway can deter ships, increase insurance costs and push companies toward alternative routes.
The next Iranian moves will therefore be critical. Tehran's pledge to punish the aggressor came as the IRGC reported casualties in the Larak Island attack, creating pressure on Iranian leaders to demonstrate that US attacks will carry a price.
Ralby cautioned that any escalation may not remain confined to Hormuz. He said the region has multiple potential flashpoints and warned that frustration with the status quo could lead one of the parties to act in a way that triggers renewed violence.
“The situation in Hormuz is unlikely to be resolved anytime soon,” Ralby said. “There are short tempers and short fuses among a number of the players.”
Iran has often attacked US bases across the region, Ralby noted, while the involvement of the Houthis and piracy incidents create additional opportunities for violence. The next escalation could therefore spread “well beyond the geographic confines of the strait of Hormuz.”
He also pointed to Lebanon and Gaza as flashpoints where continuing violence could prompt Iran or the Houthis to attack in new ways.
“So this thing could spiral further out of control than it has at any moment,” Ralby said.
Global Economic Stakes Rise
The consequences of a prolonged disruption in Hormuz would extend well beyond the military confrontation. Ralby said the global economic picture is becoming increasingly concerning as the Northern Hemisphere approaches winter and heating-oil demand is expected to rise.
He warned that the problem could shift from higher energy prices to questions of physical supply and potential shortages, depending on the severity of the winter.
“We become closer and closer to the winter period for the northern hemisphere with a demand for heating oil will start to spike in the next two months,” Ralby said, raising concerns about “not just price but supply and then overall shortage.”
China could add another layer of uncertainty. Ralby said Beijing has been artificially decreasing its demand for oil, but a renewed increase in Chinese consumption could send oil prices higher and deepen the economic effects of the standoff.
He warned that such pressure could also encourage more states to conduct transactions with China outside the dollar-based financial mechanisms that have helped underpin US economic influence for decades.
A Fragile Status Quo
For now, the central question is whether the August 30 strike and the IRGC retaliation remain isolated exchanges or become the start of another cycle of escalation.
Washington has shown that its effort to protect navigation extends beyond clearing mines from shipping routes. It is also prepared to strike Iranian military assets when it believes they are being used to threaten the waterway.
Iran, meanwhile, retains the ability to keep commercial shipping at risk without necessarily attempting a conventional blockade. That leaves Hormuz in an unstable middle ground: physically open, but with traffic severely constrained by the threat of attack.
Plitsas said that status quo could persist for some time if neither side returns to large-scale combat. But Ralby's warning about regional flashpoints and the economic pressure building around Hormuz underscores how difficult it may be to contain the conflict indefinitely.
The immediate test will be how Washington responds to the latest Iranian retaliation in Jordan. The longer-term challenge is whether the US can make the waterway sufficiently secure for commercial operators without triggering a wider war.

articles.title: Putin Looks To Set Russia As Counterweight To West At Bishkek Summit
articles.body:
Facing increasing confrontations with the West, Russian President Vladimir Putin looks eastward to bolster his country's standing in the region -- including with Iran -- at a major summit in Bishkek, the Kyrgyz capital.
Putin is set to hold bilateral meetings with Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, among at least seven others, starting August 31 on the sidelines of the two-day Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), which is celebrating its 25th anniversary.
Putin is also expected to hold bilateral sessions with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of non-SCO nation Turkey.
Kremlin officials said Putin has at least nine bilateral meetings scheduled as Moscow looks to place Russia as a counterweight to Western influence in the region.
Putin and Xi have often used SCO gatherings to put up a united front against Western influence in the region. Xi arrived late on August 30 and held his first meeting with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, who will serve as host of the summit.
Along with Russia, Iran, India, and China, the SCO grouping consists of Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan. Not all members are allies, of course, with nuclear powers Pakistan and India often on the brink of war with each other.
Originally The 'Shanghai Five'
The organization began as the "Shanghai Five" in 1996 but began expanding to other regional nations starting in 2001.
Moscow and Tehran are both under crippling Western sanctions -- Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and Iran for a multitude of issues, including its support for extremist activity in the Middle East and its alleged pursuit of a nuclear weapon.
Kyiv and the West have demanded that Iran cease from providing deadly Shahed drones to Russia for use in the Ukraine war, while US officials told RFE/RL that Russia is providing Iran with targeting information to attack US troops and military assets in the Middle East, confirming a Washington Post report.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said "one of the key subjects" in the talks between Putin and Pezeshkian will be the Middle East crisis. "You know how relevant this meeting is in light of the current uneasy atmosphere in the Middle East and the situation surrounding Iran," he added.
Also on the agenda will be the $25 billion agreement signed by Tehran with Russia's state nuclear company Rosatom to build four nuclear power plants in Iran.
Naser al-Tamimi, a UK-based analyst and founder of MidEast Strategia, wrote on X that the SCO can help largely isolated Iran, "but only to a point."
"The SCO offers Iran broader political cover, helps reduce its international isolation and expands opportunities for trade and settlements in yuan, rubles and other national currencies. In doing so, it can modestly reduce Tehran’s dependence on the Western financial system."
"But the SCO is not an economic shield against US sanctions. It lacks a fully developed alternative financial architecture, provides no reliable protection for major banks and companies exposed to secondary sanctions, and cannot compel China or India to absorb high economic costs on Iran’s behalf."
UN Chief Expected
Along with Turkey, other nonmember nations and others participating and observing will include Armenia, Azerbaijan, UN chief Antonio Guterres, and heads of several Moscow-oriented international organizations.
Putin is scheduled to meet Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian, whose country has long been an ally of Russia but which has angered Moscow by seeking to move closer to the West.
Tensions heightened between the two countries after Armenian police on August 25 arrested former President Robert Kocharian, now leader of the country’s second-largest opposition party, amid accusations of corruption-related offenses.
Kocharian, 71, served as Armenia's president between 1998 and 2008. He currently leads the Armenia Alliance, which is considered pro-Moscow and finished third in recent parliamentary elections in June.
Yerevan has also angered Moscow by its recent expressions of the desire to eventually join the European Union.
"We will insist that Armenia cannot aspire for EU membership while hugely benefiting from cooperation within the European Economic Union (EEU)," said Ushakov, referring to the five-member trade bloc that also includes Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan.
Following the Bishkek event, Putin is scheduled to travel to Vladivostok for the Eastern Economic Forum on Russia's Pacific coast from September 1-4.
He is also set to meet with leaders of several other countries there, including the Indonesian president and Mongolian prime minister.

articles.title: Russia threatens mass strikes on Ukraine energy sites as Kyiv depot death toll hits 38
articles.body:
As Moscow warns of a fresh bombing campaign and Kyiv absorbs one of the deadliest strikes to hit its own soil since the invasion began, four years of fighting show no sign of nearing a diplomatic end.
Russia's defence ministry says it is preparing large-scale strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, framing the move as retaliation for Kyiv's attacks on Russian territory, as the death toll from a Russian strike on an ammunition depot near the Ukrainian capital climbed to 38.
"The Russian Armed Forces have begun preparations for massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in response to what Moscow describes as ongoing attacks by the Kyiv regime on Russia’s civilian infrastructure and fuel and energy facilities," the defence ministry in Moscow said on Telegram.
The warning revives fears of a repeat of last winter, when Moscow's bombardment of Ukrainian power plants devastated the country's grid and left millions without heat or electricity in sub-zero temperatures.
Both sides have escalated long-range strikes over the past several months, hitting warehouses, refineries, ports and ships, with rising civilian casualties.
Depot strike toll climbs to 38
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday that the death toll from Saturday's Russian drone strike on a munitions depot in the village of Myla, in the Bucha district near Kyiv, had risen to 38, with 20 people injured and four still missing. Writing on Telegram, Zelensky said "the extent of contamination in the area is significant" as emergency crews worked to extinguish the remaining fires and bomb disposal teams cleared the site.
The strike triggered a massive detonation and secondary explosions that sent flames into surrounding residential areas, damaging around 50 buildings and forcing the evacuation of more than 380 residents, according to regional officials. Among the dead was Taras Didych, mayor of the nearby village of Dmytrivka. It is one of the deadliest single incidents Kyiv's suburbs have seen since Russia's full-scale invasion began more than four years ago.
Ukrainian prosecutors have opened a criminal negligence investigation focused on why explosives were being stored so close to homes.
A third day of sustained attacks
The Myla strike capped a third consecutive day of Russian aerial bombardment — among the most sustained since spring.
Russia's military said it also struck a cement and asbestos plant in Kyiv on Sunday, alleging its warehouses were being used to store explosives, along with a drone and munitions manufacturing site.
Overall, Russia launched two Iskander-M ballistic missiles and 130 drones of various types between late Saturday and early Sunday, the Ukrainian air force said.
Ukraine, for its part, struck an oil refinery in northwestern Russia with drones, sparking a fire, according to local Russian authorities.
The Kirishi oil refinery in Russia’s Leningrad region is the country's second-largest production plant, with the capacity to process around 20 million tonnes of crude oil a year for jet fuel and diesel.
Kyiv has increasingly targeted Russia's energy and oil infrastructure — refineries, pumping stations and storage depots — as part of a strategy officials say is meant to pressure Moscow economically toward ending the war.

articles.title: Ukraine is testing four new drone interceptors as Russia floods its skies with faster Gerans
articles.body:
Ukraine has four potential interceptor systems that could shoot down Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered Geran attack drones, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on 30 August, according to Suspilne.
Russia has sharply increased its use of the faster drones against Ukrainian cities, causing major damage to civilian infrastructure and many civilian casualties. The attacks are putting near-unprecedented strain on Ukraine’s air defenses.
All four interceptor systems have undergone field testing, Khmara said. Ukraine now aims to bring them to the required level as quickly as possible and scale production to thousands of units.
“The search for countermeasures against jet-powered drones continues,” Khmara told journalists, according to Suspilne. “There are already four potential interceptors that can shoot down jet-powered ‘Shaheds.’ Field tests have already been conducted on them.”
Russia is rapidly expanding Geran attacks
Russia's Gerans are jet-powered adaptations of the Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones that Russia has produced domestically throughout the full-scale war. The faster Geran variants give Ukrainian air defenses less time to detect and engage them.
Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said Russia used more than 2,500 jet-powered Gerans against Ukraine in August, up from about 1,500 in July.
He also said the drones are being launched against Ukraine almost directly from Russian factories, highlighting the rapid expansion of their production and use.
Zelenskyy calls for faster production
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has made countering the Gerans a priority as Russia sustains repeated attacks on Ukrainian cities.
At a 28 August meeting of Ukraine’s military leadership, Zelenskyy said the country needed to maximize domestic weapons production, with the immediate focus on defending against jet-powered Gerans and increasing Ukraine’s own long-range strikes against Russia.
“[The] main thing is our defense against jet-powered ‘Shaheds,’” Zelenskyy said in his evening address.
He said Russia had adopted a tactic of keeping Kyiv and other cities under repeated air raid alerts, with Gerans reaching the capital as well as cities including Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia.
Four days of Russian attacks keep Kyiv under near-constant fire. Ukraine is struggling to defend its skies
“All our means of countering [them] are already being used,” Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine needs a significant acceleration in production of interceptors specifically designed for the jet-powered drones.
Khmara said the four potential interceptors are now at the field-testing stage, with the next step being to bring them into production at a scale of thousands of units.
For Ukraine, that scale is critical. The country must defend a large territory against increasingly large Russian drone barrages while also preserving limited air-defense resources for ballistic and other missiles that require more advanced interceptors.

articles.title: Middle East Live: US strikes Iran for first time in a month, Tehran retaliates
articles.body:
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in their first military action in a month on Sunday, breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months. Iran swiftly vowed to retaliate for what it called a deadly attack. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Jordan army says intercepted eight missiles
Jordan's army said Monday it had intercepted eight missiles, shortly after Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had attacked US military targets in the Washington-allied kingdom.
"Air defense systems intercepted eight missiles that breached the Kingdom's airspace at dawn today, Monday," read a statement quoting the army's spokesperson.
Iran's IRGC says it launched attack on two US bases in Jordan
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Monday they attacked US military targets in Jordan, state media reported.
The Guards "targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities, and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and Al-Azraq airbases in Jordan" with ballistic missiles, causing "heavy damage", according to a statement published by state TV.
Iran Guards promise 'reprisals' after deadly US strikes
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said that US strikes on an island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday had left dead and wounded and promised reprisals.
The US strike, which hit Iran's Larak Island, was the first such attack in a month.
A statement from US Central Command said that Iran's Revolutionary Guards had been observed "preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz".
Vessels crossing Strait of Hormuz drop to 5 per day over weekend
The number of visible commodity vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz dropped to five per day over the weekend, shipping data showed on Monday, as companies tread cautiously amid continued attacks on ships.
The actual number of ships passing the strait could be higher as some vessels have switched off their automatic identification system to evade attacks.
Weekend traffic was limited to small-sized vessels, data from commodities firm Kpler showed. These included two liquefied petroleum gas carriers with one of them exiting the strait via the Iranian route while the other sailed out in the dark and is heading for India, the data showed.
Iran is attacking US forces in Jordan, Fox News reports, citing a US source
Iran is attacking US forces stationed in Jordan, Fox News reporter Trey Yingst said on Sunday, citing a US source.
There has been no significant impact so far, the reporter's X post said, adding that nearly all incoming missiles "have been intercepted at this point."
Oil jumps more than 2% after US attack on Iran's Larak island
Oil prices jumped more than 2% on Monday, with Brent back above $90 a barrel, after US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Iran's Larak island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, the first known American strikes on the Gulf nation since late July.
US plans to sanction another bank in effort to clamp down on Iran transactions
The Trump administration plans to impose sanctions on another bank this week in an effort to clamp down on Iran transactions, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday.
Bessent spoke with The Associated Press ahead of Group of 20 meetings in Asheville, North Carolina, where he will meet individually with his counterparts from the world’s major and developing economies to encourage participation in the economic isolation of Iran.
“This is going to be financial violence if we have to,” Bessent said in the interview. “We are showing people that we know who you are, you know who you are, and this has got to stop.”

articles.title: US military attacked IRGC rocket launchers in Iran, senior official confirms
articles.body:
A senior U.S. official said Sunday evening that the U.S. military struck two Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps rocket launchers on Larak Island. 
“The two launchers were preparing to fire missiles carrying naval mines toward the Strait of Hormuz,” the official told Reuters and other news outlets. “Our forces have completed clearing mines from international shipping lanes, are closely monitoring the area and are prepared to defend the free flow of commerce through the strait.”
Iran’s Fars news agency reported that an explosion was heard near Larak Island in the strait.
The Tasnim news agency reported that according to "Preliminary, unofficial reports" two people were killed and two others were injured in the American attack.  
Shortly after the attack, the Revolutionary Guards threatened that "the enemy's terrorist act of aggression on Larak Island will be met with a response, and the aggressor will be punished."
"The American-Zionist enemy, once again driven by desperation in solving its internal problems and reducing its credibility among regional countries, seeks to revive its nefarious role and justify public opinion. In a blatant act of aggression, it attacked Larak Island, resulting in the martyrdom and injury of several of our soldiers and fellow citizens," the IRGC also said in a statement.
The Washington Post reported Sunday that senior U.S. military commanders had warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that large-scale operations against Iran could not be sustained over time, and that continuing to concentrate forces in the Middle East could impair the U.S. military’s ability to deal with threats elsewhere in the world, including defending the United States itself.
According to officials familiar with the classified assessment prepared for Hegseth, the warnings were delivered to the defense secretary by the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force, as well as commanders of U.S. forces responsible for Europe, Asia and Latin America. They were included in the August 14 edition of the “Secretary of Defense Orders Book,” a classified document detailing the availability of U.S. ships, aircraft, troops and weapons systems around the world that the Pentagon uses in making force-deployment decisions.
The strike in the strait came after about six months of fighting with Iran, as U.S. President Donald Trump pressures Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and accept Washington’s terms for ending the conflict. Trump continues to make clear that all options remain on the table, including renewed strikes, and U.S. Central Command, or CENTCOM, has for months kept more than 50,000 troops on alert in case the president orders further military action.
According to the Post, some of the forces deployed to the Middle East have already been ordered to remain in the region through September, while others are expected to stay into 2027. The Air Force is also preparing for a prolonged presence: According to two officials who saw the document, many of the units sent to the Middle East for bombing missions and round-the-clock operations are expected to remain in the region into 2027.
The possibility that the deployments could be extended again prompted several senior commanders to voice explicit objections. The commanders of U.S. European Command, Indo-Pacific Command and Southern Command, along with the Navy’s top officer, submitted what the Pentagon calls a “non-concur” — meaning they oppose the defense secretary’s decision to extend the allocation of their forces to the campaign, though they would carry out the order if it remains in effect.

articles.title: Ukraine’s war didn’t go to plan. Its former defense minister’s career did
articles.body:
Ukraine’s war didn’t go to plan. Its former defense minister’s career did
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov has suddenly – and rather unexpectedly – become an adviser to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto. The news caught many conservative military analysts off guard. Why would Italy want him, and what does Rome hope to gain? Let’s try to make sense of the move without getting carried away.
A manager in khaki, not a marshal
It should be obvious that Fedorov is no military genius, nor does he possess any particular talent as a battlefield commander. That is simply not who he is. He was never a career officer, and he never made his name drawing thick red arrows across maps of future operations. First and foremost, Mikhail Fedorov is an effective IT executive – and a knowledgeable chief customer for the entire defense industry.
His path to that role began as the top digital strategist for Vladimir Zelensky’s presidential campaign, where he built an online campaign network and bet heavily on internet marketing. From there, he went on to create Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation and roll out the Diia digital ecosystem, which changed everyday life across the country. In 2026, Fedorov took over the Defense Ministry amid an urgent need to impose order and bring sweeping digitalization to the armed forces. The timing, it seems, could hardly have been better.
Several major changes in the Ukrainian military were introduced with Fedorov’s involvement:
- Drone procurement for military units was radically overhauled through the launch of a dedicated marketplace designed to minimize red tape. It was a highly unconventional move that significantly shortened the path from manufacturer to frontline unit while opening up a market for many small and relatively young companies. After drones, the same digital approach began spreading to other parts of the defense industry.
- Agile management methods were effectively brought into military life, breaking down long-established systems of multistage approval and allowing new ideas to be tested quickly under real battlefield conditions – directly in the trenches.
- The military opened its doors to software developed by civilian companies. The emphasis shifted toward finding new and unconventional solutions that could be deployed quickly and deliver results immediately, rather than waiting for lengthy testing reports and reviews by specialized military institutes.
Of course, Fedorov’s role in these changes should not be overstated. Many of the initiatives that reshaped the Ukrainian military began before he arrived at the Defense Ministry. What he brought was a fresh, digital perspective that helped cut some corners and speed up the adoption of new ideas.
There were no combat operations or battlefield triumphs involved. He was a digital-solutions manager who put on a military uniform – focused exclusively on digital systems and a project-based approach to reform. And naturally the process was not without its rough edges. Digitalization remains the only clear success he can point to.
Why Rome wants the “Ukraine playbook”
Perhaps that is precisely what Rome needs: not military victories or battlefield credentials, but a fresh, modern approach. That, presumably, is where Italy is placing its hopes. Modern European militaries, including Italy’s, are weighed down by bureaucracy. Decisions on the procurement of new weapons systems and software take years. By the time they are finally approved, technology has already moved on, leaving armed forces to adopt systems that were obsolete before they ever entered service.
Fedorov may well be useful to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto as a new battering ram against his own conservative military establishment. Rome wants to borrow Ukraine’s experience of rapidly digitalizing military logistics and integrating unmanned systems in real time.
To understand exactly which processes Fedorov may seek to adapt for the Italian military, one need only look inside his “digital briefcase.” It contains no secret missile technology – only commercial software and civilian IT solutions adapted to the needs of a defense ministry.
The Italian military is eager to introduce new digital battle-management systems that combine geospatial tools with hundreds of information sources and a distributed network of users, extending from the General Staff all the way to a frontline commander’s tablet in the trenches. Italy is also naturally interested in digitalizing weapons and military-equipment procurement – and even more so in applying artificial intelligence to military command and control.
It is difficult to judge the results, but on paper Fedorov’s résumé looks highly impressive: experience introducing cutting-edge digital solutions in Europe’s only army currently fighting a major war. That is certainly one way to present it – and why be shy when listing your strengths on a résumé?
What Rome is really buying
A modern army increasingly resembles an IT corporation. Rome does not need Fedorov’s advice on how to defend its coastline or plan an armored offensive. It needs his ability to turn the military into a functioning digital platform.
But let’s take an honest look at the former defense minister’s record. Yes, there was digitalization and digital transformation. It may still be too early to assess the final results, but there have been no major successes on the battlefield – and that, one would think, is what an army is ultimately for and how its performance should be measured.
Then there is the less flattering part of the picture: the image of a petulant child who could not find common ground with career officers and began playing political games in the middle of an ongoing war to increase his own value back home. That hardly seems consistent with the image of a gifted digital manager. Wars, after all, are not won through digitalization alone, but through the coordinated action of different branches and types of forces.
It will be fascinating to see what Fedorov ‘achieves’ in his new job – and whether the spirit of Silicon Valley can take root in the austere offices of the Italian Defense Ministry.
As for the man with the polished résumé and the reputation of a ‘digitalization expert’, a position like this – especially in Rome – offers a splendid opportunity to make a graceful exit from Kiev and trade Ukraine’s brutal political reality for the warm, easygoing comforts of Europe.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: America lost its longest war five years ago. This is what victory looks like for the Taliban
articles.body:
America lost its longest war five years ago. This is what victory looks like for the Taliban
“When Ashraf Ghani goes, we’ll go with him. And he’ll go when the Americans do.”
The conversation took place on the balcony of a luxury high-rise in Shahr-e Naw, central Kabul. The man speaking to me was a young government employee, and Ashraf Ghani was serving his second term as president of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan. It was May 2017. The republic had four years and three months left.
A city living on borrowed time
Afghanistan at the time could best be described with a line from Dickens: “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times… we had everything before us, we had nothing before us.” Kabul was both deeply Westernized and full of contradictions. The former was fueled by the abundance of foreigners and foreign aid; the latter by the unending fighting and terrorist attacks.
Downtown, you could find nightclubs throwing Valentine’s Day and Halloween parties, modeling agencies, coffee shops serving cheesecake, bowling alleys, and tattoo parlors. On the outskirts, tent camps were expanding to accommodate internally displaced people – refugees from the provinces, mostly in the south, whose homes had been destroyed by the war. Street boys begged in English: “Give me one hundred dollars!” Artists painted murals warning about domestic violence, fashionable women wore jeans and bright makeup, and Western NGOs taught Afghan children to skateboard.
At the same time, some places – including the park in Shahr-e Naw itself – were unsafe even in broad daylight because of the number of drug addicts, while robberies and kidnappings had become routine. After sunset, the city shut down. Several years later, The New York Times would call Kabul a city of hope and despair – an apt metaphor.
To protect itself from the constant bombings, Kabul grew a shell of concrete walls and checkpoints. There seemed to be as many police officers and soldiers on the streets as civilians, while American surveillance balloons hovered continuously over the city. None of it helped much. That same May, while I was there, a tanker truck packed with explosives detonated in the diplomatic quarter, killing more than 90 people and wounding around 400. Smaller incidents had long since ceased to qualify as news. One of my editors gave me a simple rule:
“If there’s a terrorist attack in Kabul and fewer than ten people are killed, don’t write about it. That’s not news.”
Politics and public life were no less remarkable. Afghanistan’s parliament had as many women as the US Congress, yet in the center of the capital a mob lynched Farkhunda Malikzada, a young Afghan woman, after a mullah falsely accused her of burning the Quran. Corruption broke every record, and the central government was weak. Hamid Karzai, the republic’s first president, had been dubbed the “president of Kabul.” Ashraf Ghani was already merely the “president of the presidential palace.” A provincial governor removed from office could simply declare that the president had no authority over him and remain at his post. Drug production reached unprecedented levels: according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, 84% of the opiates on the global market in 2017 originated in Afghanistan.
This was what years of NATO’s military presence had made of the country and its capital. Once the troops withdrew, the existing order was bound to collapse.
The war that kept changing uniforms
The arrival of the United States and its allies in Afghanistan opened a new chapter in a civil war that, with varying degrees of intensity, had already been raging for 23 years.
Pandora’s box was opened in 1978, when the left came to power. The United States, Pakistan, China, and the Gulf states began actively arming the opposition, while the new government asked the Soviet Union for help. From 1979 to 1989, the Limited Contingent of Soviet Forces carried out what Moscow called its “internationalist duty” in Afghanistan, supporting a friendly government and controlling the major cities and some of the roads – the most any foreign army could hope to hold in the country’s mountainous terrain.
After the Soviet withdrawal, Mohammad Najibullah’s pro-Soviet government survived for roughly four years before being overthrown by the mujahideen: warlords who had first fought the shuravi – “Soviets” in Dari – and then turned their guns on one another in a struggle for power. The Taliban entered Kabul in 1996, bringing down the mujahideen government everywhere except the Panjshir Valley. The international community then forgot about Afghanistan for five years. It remembered the country only after the September 11, 2001 attacks, because Osama bin Laden was hiding there.
Immediately after the attacks came an episode recounted in ethnography classes to every student specializing in Afghanistan. George W. Bush issued the Taliban an ultimatum: hand over bin Laden. They refused. The official explanation was that there was no evidence linking him to the attacks. But there was an unofficial reason as well: bin Laden was a guest in Afghanistan. For the Pashtuns – the country’s largest ethnic group, to which the Taliban also belong – the rules of hospitality are sacred, and surrendering a guest to his enemy would bring shame for generations.
Uninterested in the finer points of the local mindset, Bush spent a month bombing Afghanistan and destroying the Taliban’s air force and air defenses. Then came the ground operation, first carried out with the help of allied forces – the same mujahideen – and later by US Marines under Operation Enduring Freedom. The United States had entered the longest war in its history and, at the same time, decided to build a democracy in Afghanistan – a bold idea for a country still living, in many respects, in the Middle Ages, with only a third of its population able to read and write. American filmmakers would later explore the absurdity of the situation and Washington’s profound failure to understand the country in War Machine, starring Brad Pitt.
For the first several years, things went reasonably well. Hamid Karzai, mentioned above, was elected president, a parliament was elected, and the United Nations and other international organizations threw themselves into reconstruction. While much of the money ended up in officials’ pockets, life did improve in some respects: child mortality declined, and the number of young women attending universities rose.
By 2005, however, the Taliban had recovered from their defeat and launched a guerrilla war in the south, where they found no shortage of supporters. Again, I think back to those university ethnography classes. We were taught that Afghans prefer something of their own, even if it is bad, to something good imposed by outsiders. In other words, Afghans have always hated occupiers. NATO troops – who periodically stormed into the women’s quarters of homes during raids or killed civilians, whether by mistake or out of fear – were no exception. The Taliban, for all their conservatism and radical methods, were still their own. Their values did not clash with those of Afghanistan’s rural heartland. I still remember how Taliban fighters were welcomed in Kabul during a three-day ceasefire in 2018: people gave them flowers, took selfies with them, brought them food, hugged them, and wept.
During the years of the American presence, much of the resentment toward the Soviet Union had faded.
”Yes, you fought us, but you fought well, like men,” former mujahideen told me again and again in different parts of the country. “You were brave: face to face, and the stronger man won. But these people? They bomb us from airplanes.”
The runway at the end of the world
On August 15, 2021, a message from Kabul woke me. It was from an Afghan journalist I knew.
”They’re here.”
“Who?”
“The Taliban. They’ve taken the city. It’s over.”
I had flown out of Kabul in February, and that assignment had been my bleakest: three or four explosions a day, activists and politicians being assassinated, Taliban patrols operating barely 12 miles from the capital. Kabul was practically under siege. Intense localized fighting raged in the south, official figures put the death toll at a hundred people a day, and provincial capitals kept changing hands.
Biden had announced that American troops would leave Afghanistan by September 11 – the irony was hard to miss – but analysts remained fairly optimistic. After all, Najibullah had held on for several years. Why couldn’t Ghani? Operation Enduring Freedom had long since been replaced by the noncombat Resolute Support mission, with alliance troops training and advising their Afghan counterparts so they could stand up to the Taliban on their own. Depending on the forecast, the republic was expected to survive anywhere from two to six months.
The Afghan armed forces did, in fact, have plenty of combat-ready units: Special Forces and commando brigades, as well as the Grom and Gardez regional army corps based in Khost and Kandahar. But every conversation I had with the military left me with the same heavy feeling. Many complained that both their allies and their commanders were indifferent to their fate, while morale in more remote areas was catastrophically low. The commander of a checkpoint in Kunar Province told me he had gone several months without food, ammunition, or pay. Of the eight soldiers under his command, three were suffering from depression. One no longer got out of bed and was preparing to die, even though his wound was not serious; he was also using drugs. Two others were planning to defect to the Taliban. Every evening, the militants used loudspeakers to urge them to surrender, promising to spare their lives – a common practice at the time, and the Taliban generally kept their word. The commander himself, though “tired to death,” as he put it, had no intention of giving up. He had killed too many of them to expect mercy.
”No one will fight for the president. Nobody likes him,” he told me as we said goodbye. “And the president wouldn’t fight for us, either. The Americans deceived him, and he’ll deceive us.”
His words about the president proved prophetic: Ashraf Ghani fled to Uzbekistan before Kabul had even fallen fully under Taliban control. But the checkpoint commander was wrong about his own future. He survived the fall of the government and became a taxi driver. Tens of thousands of his former comrades found work as security guards, construction workers, shopkeepers, or day laborers. The new government granted them amnesty but did not trust them enough to keep them in the army.
But back to the morning of August 15. Mass panic gripped Kabul. A crowd rushed to the airport – the only place still under coalition control – tore down the barriers, and flooded the tarmac. Terrified people tried to force their way onto American planes, and their fear was entirely understandable: many remembered the public executions and ethnic cleansing of the Taliban’s first period in power. Photographs from Kabul in August 2021 bore an uncanny resemblance to those from Saigon in April 1975, when the Americans were also evacuating their allies. History does, after all, have a way of moving in circles. Kabul itself, incidentally, fell without a fight. Among those who spent weeks waiting for a flight and sleeping on the runways were many former members of the security forces who had gone home without firing a shot and hidden their uniforms.
”American troops cannot and should not be fighting in a war and dying in a war that Afghan forces are not willing to fight for themselves,” US President Joe Biden said in summing up the debacle.
”We were betrayed,” General Sami Sadat, a deputy commander of the Afghan army, told The New York Times.
Analysts now expected mass reprisals and another round of civil war. But Afghanistan – now the Islamic Emirate – was quiet.
A different kind of silence
A teapot filled with green tea sits on the desk of a Taliban official at the Ministry of Information. My hospitable host diligently keeps my cup full, pushes a dish of chewy candies toward me, and asks what I think of the new government. A month and a half has passed since the fall of the republic – or the “victory,” as the Taliban themselves call it.
”Have you been to our country before?”
“Yes.”
“And when was it better – then or now?”
“It’s much safer now,” I say. It is clearly the answer he expects, and one I can give with a clear conscience.
This time I arrived in Kabul from the north, after a 12-hour drive from Mazar-i-Sharif through the Salang Pass. Under the republic, such a journey would have been unthinkable. Fighting had raged all along the road. The reminders were everywhere: burned-out army vehicles stacked in pyramids, the walls of homes blown away by explosions, and the road itself, pocked with craters from mines and shelling. You can now walk at night in any part of Kabul, though few Afghans take advantage of the opportunity. No one yet understands what to expect from the new rulers. People fear them, despite all the leaders’ talk of peace and brotherhood. Yet after events that many Afghans experienced as the end of the world, life slipped back into its familiar rhythms with surprising speed. Government offices and banks were operating, stores were open, and there were no fewer women on the streets – and not all of them were wrapped in the famous blue burqas. The worst fears had not come true, at least not at that point.
”Just give us time,” the Taliban official says with a smile. “After the revolution, the Bolsheviks needed time to accomplish something, too.” He calls them “the Communists.” “Come back in five years, and everything will be different.”
And now, almost five years later, I do see Afghanistan again.
It is still quiet here, despite the conflict with Pakistan and divisions within the leadership. But it is a different kind of quiet.
The Emirate has many enemies, and its security services are exceptionally vigilant. To the Taliban, every foreigner is a potential spy. Tourists, reporters, and the staff of the humanitarian missions still operating in the country are kept under constant surveillance, while Afghans who speak with them can face trouble, up to and including arrest. The religious police, meanwhile, enforce compliance with Sharia. The sticks in the officers’ hands may be mostly for show, but people still try not to attract their attention.
Music is banned. There are many prohibitions, and a good number of them concern perfectly innocent things such as chess, which is now considered a form of gambling. The craters left by explosions have long since been patched. Restaurants that look far more like Dubai than Kabul are opening in Shahr-e Naw. The drug addicts were forcibly removed from the park long ago and sent to treatment centers that have almost no medicine. Girls still have not returned to school since the takeover, and working women are almost nowhere to be seen. No, unlike the republic, the Islamic Emirate is not a place of contradictions, and Kabul stopped being a city of despair long ago. But there is little hope left in it, either.
Downtown, the concrete walls are being dismantled. They are no longer needed now that the bombings have stopped. The republic-era murals have faded so badly that the words “We Want Peace” are barely legible. And Afghanistan has, indeed, enjoyed its longest stretch of peace in 40 years.

articles.title: Iran fires ballistic missiles at US bases in Jordan
articles.body:
Iran said Monday it launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. bases in Jordan in retaliation for an American strike on Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, marking a new escalation in the months-long conflict between Washington and Tehran.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said ballistic missiles targeted U.S. forces at the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan, according to Iranian media.
Jordan’s armed forces said Monday they intercepted eight missiles that entered Jordanian airspace, state television reported.
The launches followed reports Sunday that Iran was attacking U.S. forces stationed in Jordan. Fox News correspondent Trey Yingst, citing a U.S. source, said there had been no significant impact and that nearly all incoming missiles had been intercepted at that point.
The Revolutionary Guards said Monday’s missile attack was retaliation for a U.S. strike Sunday on Larak Island, a strategically located Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.
A senior U.S. official said the American military struck two IRGC rocket launchers on the island that were preparing to fire missiles carrying naval mines toward the Strait of Hormuz. The official said U.S. forces had finished clearing mines from international shipping lanes and were prepared to protect commercial navigation through the strategic waterway.
Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported preliminary, unofficial figures of two people killed and two wounded in the U.S. strike. Shortly afterward, the Revolutionary Guards vowed that the attack would be met with a response and that the United States would be punished.
The confrontation comes after about six months of fighting with Iran as President Donald Trump presses Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and accept U.S. terms for ending the conflict. U.S. Central Command has kept more than 50,000 troops on alert in the region for months amid the possibility of further military action.
