A Russian State Duma deputy called for the use of nuclear weapons against Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Aleksey Zhuravlyov called for the use of tactical nuclear weapons against Ukraine to force its capitulation. There are no signs of preparations for a strike.
Russian State Duma deputy and leader of the Rodina party Alexei Zhuravlyov called for the use of tactical nuclear weapons against Ukraine to force it to capitulate. The Moscow Times reports this, citing a statement by the Russian parliamentarian, writes UNN.
Details
According to Zhuravlyov, there should allegedly be no discussion in Russia at all about the possibility of using tactical nuclear weapons.
If necessary, we are obliged to use them. If we have to strike, we will strike. And this is not up for discussion
There are currently no signs of preparations for a nuclear strike
Earlier, Bloomberg, citing sources close to the Kremlin, reported that Vladimir Putin might view tactical nuclear weapons as a last resort in the event of a sharp deterioration in Russia’s position. At the same time, the outlet emphasized that there were no signs of Moscow preparing to use them.
Russia’s partners also oppose such a scenario. In particular, according to media reports, China warned the Kremlin against using nuclear weapons.
Zhuravlyov’s statement came amid new reports of attempts by the United States to persuade Moscow to abandon further escalation and return to negotiations on ending the hostilities.

articles.title: Death toll from Russian strike on Bucha district rises – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Death toll from Russian strike on Bucha district rises – Zelenskyy
The death toll from a Russian strike and subsequent detonations in the village of Myla in Kyiv Oblast has risen to 38, and another 20 people have been injured.
Source: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
Details: Zelenskyy said two children are among those injured. Another four people are missing, and the search for them is ongoing.
Rescue workers are operating at the scene around the clock. Most fires caused by the attack have been extinguished, and State Emergency Service bomb disposal teams are identifying and neutralising explosive objects.
Zelenskyy noted that the area remains heavily contaminated with explosive objects.
The president also said that over the past week, Russia has used nearly 2,000 attack drones, more than 1,600 aerial bombs and 31 missiles of various types, including North Korean ballistic missiles, against Ukraine.
Background:
- Powerful explosions were heard in the Bucha district of Kyiv Oblast on the evening of 28 August. A warehouse facility caught fire, and all traffic was blocked in both directions on the M-06 Kyiv-Chop road between kilometres 15 and 32.
- As of 29 August, local authorities reported that the death toll from the Russian attack and subsequent detonation in the Bucha district had risen to 37, while another 42 people were injured.
- Zelenskyy stated that ammunition cannot be stored near residential buildings. He also said the first strike in Myla village hit a defence forces warehouse that "should not have been there".
- Commenting on the deaths of dozens of people after the Russian strike on Myla, Ukraine's General Staff said Russia is the root cause of the tragedy.

articles.body:
The President of Finland does not believe in Russia's attack on NATO and rules out a nuclear strike on Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Alexander Stubb said that he sees no evidence of Russia preparing to attack NATO. He also doubts that there will be a nuclear strike on Ukraine.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb said he sees no evidence of a possible Russian attack on NATO, and also expressed doubt that Moscow would use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. BILD reports, writes UNN.
I do not believe that Russia will ever want to attack the world's most powerful military alliance — NATO
He commented on Germany's warning that Russia could be capable of attacking NATO territory by 2029, noting that he sees "neither evidence nor facts" supporting such a scenario.
According to Stubb, NATO has a powerful deterrent based on conventional forces, missiles, and nuclear weapons.
There is no point for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance
The President of Finland also expressed doubt about the possibility of a Russian nuclear strike on Ukraine. According to him, he raised the issue during a conversation with China's foreign minister, who said that China "would never allow this to happen."
At the same time, Stubb emphasized that Europe must be prepared for the worst-case scenario in order to prevent it.

Sweden to Deploy Gripen Fighter Jets and Naval Ships to Guard Finnish Border With Russia
The Swedish government has decided to send military units to Finland to strengthen patrolling operations along the border with Russia.
According to Swedish public broadcaster SVT on August 28, the action comes after a direct request from Finnish authorities for military assistance to respond to ongoing air space threats tied to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over the past year, Finland has recorded several instances of Ukrainian drones straying into its territory due to electronic warfare, alongside repeated air space violations by Russian military aircraft.
To handle these security concerns, the Swedish Armed Forces will soon deploy JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets and naval vessels to patrol regions along the Finnish-Russian border.
Additional ground support may also follow later in the year. Swedish air defense and counter-drone units could be sent to Finland during the autumn if the operational situation requires further force integration.
The entire deployment is organized alongside NATO and relies on bilateral agreements between the two nations. These legal frameworks give the Swedish government the mandate to deploy armed forces directly for the defense of Finnish territorial integrity.
This operation sits within a larger expansion of regional security ties in Northern Europe. Sweden is set to assume command of NATO forward land forces in Finland, where international troops will form a core element of the alliance's enhanced defense presence.
This framework includes a primary battalion task group stationed in Finland alongside a permanent multinational headquarters.
Previously, Sweden's parliamentary defense commission warned in a report covered by Bloomberg on June 12 that Russia could seek to test NATO's cohesion and commitment to mutual defense through a military attack in the "relatively near term."
The commission stated that such action could come if the Kremlin assessed that "political conditions are favorable," even when the balance of forces fell short of the traditional threshold for an attack, Bloomberg reported.

articles.title: 6 issues that will shape Ursula von der Leyen’s legacy
articles.body:
6 issues that will shape Ursula von der Leyen’s legacy
With 3 years left in her term, the Commission boss must revive Europe’s industry, defend its rules, bolster security, support Ukraine, expand the bloc — and pay for it all.
Ursula von der Leyen has three years left to cement her legacy, but it’ll be far from easy.
Von der Leyen’s second term ends in 2029, by which time she’ll have been at the helm of the European Commission for a decade. If, as Brussels Playbook reported earlier this summer, the EU executive chief won’t seek a third term, then she’s in the final stretch of her career in Brussels.
Her time in office has been dominated by crisis management — Covid-19, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, sky-high energy prices, war in Gaza. In the years to come, the challenges will likely keep mounting, including competition from China and the United States, and upcoming elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland that could reshape the EU.
Advertisement
In the Commission’s Berlaymont HQ, von der Leyen and her team are feverishly working on her State of the EU speech, to be delivered on Sept. 16. It’s when she will set out her plan for the years to come. After that, she’ll have to deliver.
“Speeches are important. But it’s the actions that create legacy,” said Martin Hojsík, a vice president of the European Parliament from the Renew Europe group.
“Europe has become more vulnerable economically, competitiveness remains a major challenge, social and regional inequalities persist, and too often her Commission has reacted to crises rather than anticipated them,” said Victor Negrescu, a Parliament vice president from the Socialists and Democrats group. “I expect her to use this moment to defend her record, but also to explain how Europe can deliver more on growth, investment, social cohesion and strategic autonomy. For me, the real question is not how her legacy is presented, but what concrete results Europeans will see by the end of this mandate.”
Here are six potential headaches likely to define von der Leyen’s remaining time in office.
1. Reversing Europe’s decline
Will von der Leyen be able to stem the Continent’s economic decline … or oversee the death of its industrial heartlands?
It was von der Leyen who asked former Italian PM and European Central Bank chief Mario Draghi to draw up a report into the continent’s competitiveness. He was brutal in his assessment, saying that “without action, we will have to either compromise our welfare, our environment or our freedom.” He called on Europe to invest an additional €800 billion a year to drag itself out of a trough of low productivity and feeble growth that’s pushing it behind the U.S. and China in the international pecking order.
Advertisement
Von der Leyen promised to turn Draghi’s warning into an industrial strategy, but the headwinds are strong. European companies face high energy prices, fragmented capital markets, complex regulation and intensifying competition from abroad.
And while European companies need Chinese markets and supply chains, that dependency comes at a high cost. State subsidies have allowed Chinese firms to build capacity that far exceeds domestic demand, and their EVs, batteries, solar panels and steel are putting pressure on EU rivals. Meanwhile, Beijing’s stranglehold over critical minerals used in the green transition and high-tech sectors creates vast danger.
“What you have seen with the EU position on relations with China is the status quo is far too heavily tilted in China’s favor and cannot endure,” said a Commission official, granted anonymity to speak freely. “At EU level, there’s now near-total agreement on diagnosing the problems. There is near-total agreement on what the solutions are to address those problems. The only remaining question is how robust are member states willing to be in their follow-through.”
Mario Draghi smiles after he was awarded the 2026 International Charlemagne Prize of Aachen, on May 14, 2026. | Sascha Schuermann/AFP via Getty Images
Von der Leyen’s dilemma is how to keep the Chinese market open while preventing overcapacity from hollowing out EU industry.
The Commission is overseeing a reset in China relations, while considering stronger trade-defense tools and measures to reduce supply-chain dependence. It’s a delicate balance: too much confrontation could trigger a damaging trade war; too little could leave Europe without a viable industrial base.
Brussels and Beijing are engaged in talks to resolve the issue. Trade chief Maroš Šefčovič has set an October deadline to make progress. Failure could mean that China becomes the next front in the trade war.
Advertisement
2. Protecting EU regulations from Trump
Can von der Leyen rein in Big Tech without every European decision on competition, data, digital sovereignty or child safety becoming a transatlantic confrontation?
The Digital Markets Act and Digital Services Act are in their enforcement phase, and the EU’s fines against Apple, Meta and Google have already infuriated Washington. Von der Leyen is pushing ahead with plans to restrict children under 13 from using social media, which could provoke Donald Trump further.
“We would not presume to tell the U.S. how to regulate on their sovereign territory. And that is the very fair and coherent thing we ask for in return,” said the Commission official quoted above.
3. Addressing the climate crisis while slashing green rules
The Green Deal was the defining project of von der Leyen’s first term. But with far-right forces surging around the EU and an outcry that green rules are adding to Europe’s industrial strain, von der Leyen is now being forced to undo the very policies she implemented.
If von der Leyen weakens the Green Deal too much, she risks losing credibility with citizens and her coalition partners. If she insists on ambitious rules, she could provoke more political backlash.
Advertisement
“Some environmental policies were adopted without thinking about the social issues,” acknowledged Marie Toussaint, a French Green MEP. “How to heat your home? For some people the bills are already impossible to pay. So we need to ensure that in every sector we have this social concern and we refrain from adopting anything that would worsen people’s lives.”
4. Defending Europe and Ukraine
Europe’s security debate has moved from speeches about “strategic autonomy” to the urgent question of where to get weapons and deter Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The EU is increasing defense spending, backing joint procurement and trying to expand industrial capacity through initiatives such as the €150 billion SAFE program. But national governments still disagree over how much to spend and how to spend it.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, flanked by Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, delivers a speech during a ceremony to mark the Day of Ukrainian Statehood, in Kyiv on July 15, 2026. | Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP via Getty Images
The test is whether Europe can build a defense industry that can stand on its own, given the Trump administration’s repeated undermining of NATO.
Von der Leyen will also need to ensure that Ukraine enters any potential peace negotiations with Russia in the best position possible.
“We know exactly how to talk to Russians,” said Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna. “Pressure, no compromises, and only from [a position of] strength.”
Advertisement
That means von der Leyen must ensure Ukraine gets financial and military support as well as credible long-term security guarantees, while keeping the Trump administration onside.
But while in Brussels support for Ukraine remains high, more Kremlin-friendly governments have won power around the EU, with the potential for others to join them after a series of elections in 2027, including in France and Italy.
“We operate in the real world. We have to take political reality and political developments into account in the work we do,” said the Commission official. Regardless, they added, “President von der Leyen will continue to make the case for Ukraine because that’s clearly in Europe’s best interest.”
5. Expanding the EU
Ukraine, Moldova and countries in the Western Balkans have moved closer to the EU, but political support for enlargement is not the same as readiness to admit new members.
Candidate countries must still complete difficult reforms on the rule of law, corruption and judicial independence. Current EU members worry about the cost of enlargement, future funding needs and whether the institutions can function with more than 30 members.
But von der Leyen needs to show that accession is still a credible process rather than a permanently postponed promise, before the countries in the EU’s waiting room run out of patience and look elsewhere for alliances.
Advertisement
“We deserve to be in a much more advanced position than we are right now,” North Macedonia’s Foreign Minister Timčo Mucunski said about his country’s stalled bid to join the EU. “To say that we have been treated unfairly is an understatement.”
6. Paying for it all
The EU’s next long-term budget will determine which of these headaches von der Leyen can actually treat.
The Commission proposed an almost €2 trillion budget for 2028–2034, but two entrenched camps are battling over the plan.
The so-called Friends of Cohesion — among them Italy, Greece, Poland and Spain — want more money for traditional spending areas, particularly cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy, and want those funds delivered through familiar national and regional channels.
The other camp, made up of frugal countries including Germany, Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands, wants less spending and a different allocation of cash: more for innovation, defense and European industrial capacity.
The fight collides with the political calendar.
Advertisement
A cadre of the EU’s biggest countries will hold elections in 2027, including France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Some politicians will be reluctant to explain to voters why they should send more money to Brussels; others why traditional funding should be reduced.
Yet the new EU budget (known as the Multiannual Financial Framework) must take effect on Jan. 1, 2028. That means the deal needs to be negotiated well in advance.
Von der Leyen’s second term ends in 2029. | Olivier Matthys/EPA
The closer it gets to 2027, the more domestic politics will dominate the talks — and the harder it will be to secure unanimity in the Council and consent from the European Parliament.
“When it comes to MFF negotiations, endgame negotiations are always tough, but it always gets done,” said the Commission official. “Those exact motivations [2027 elections] are fantastic factors to get the job done now.”
Eliza Gkritsi, Seb Starcevic, Max Griera and Mathieu Pollet contributed to this story.

Death toll from Russian strike on Ukrainian arms depot rises to 38
Russia’s Defence Ministry announces plans to launch ‘massive strikes’ against Ukraine’s infrastructure before winter.
The death toll from a Russian strike on an arms depot near the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, has risen to 38, marking the war’s deadliest attack so far this year, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Emergency workers on Sunday continued to extinguish the resulting fires and explosions that began on Saturday in the village of Myla, Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram, adding that bomb disposal teams were also working to clear the site.

He said 20 people were injured, while four remained missing.
The attack was the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv within two months, with officials voicing anger that arms were still being stored so close to residential areas.
Ukrainian prosecutors have opened an investigation into alleged criminal negligence.
Separately, Zelenskyy said in a video message that Kyiv is preparing for a new round of talks with representatives of US President Donald Trump, with further details expected on Monday.
Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine is “doing everything possible to ensure that war does not remain the only option for future developments”, even as Moscow intensifies its strategy of exhaustion.
“Russia’s current tactic is to wear down Ukraine, and above all, to wear down Ukrainians,” Zelenskyy said, pointing to relentless air strikes across the country.
According to the Ukrainian president, Russian forces launched nearly 1,500 drones over a four-day period, including roughly 800 jet-powered Shahed variants. He described intercepting the faster, jet-powered models as the military’s “most difficult task”.
To counter the threat, Kyiv is working to secure the necessary interceptor systems, he said. Four firms have already developed suitable interceptor drones, with technology from one company proving particularly effective, he added.
Russia warning
Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces were preparing to launch “massive strikes” against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, following a Ukrainian drone campaign against Wildberries, dubbed “Russia’s Amazon”, as well as the country’s oil and gas sector, which Kyiv says both funds and directly fuels Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
During the war’s previous winters, Russia systematically battered Ukraine’s power grid, depriving thousands of heat and light in freezing temperatures. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that the coming winter may prove the most challenging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The Ukrainian military said it launched overnight attacks on an oil refinery in Russia’s Leningrad region and a military base in the Krasnodar region.
One person was killed in a separate Ukrainian attack on a mine in the Russian-controlled part of the Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine, Moscow-installed Governor Leonid Pasechnik said.
United States-led diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, Europe’s deadliest since World War II, have been at a standstill for months.
Russia has demanded sweeping territorial and political concessions from Ukraine, which Kyiv has ruled out as tantamount to capitulation.

articles.title: CIA Director proposed a meeting between Trump, Zelenskyy and putin to end the war – Axios
articles.body:
CIA Director proposed a meeting between Trump, Zelenskyy and putin to end the war – Axios
Kyiv • UNN
John Ratcliffe proposed a trilateral summit to revive talks on the war. Ukrainian officials doubt putin’s readiness.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed holding a trilateral meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Russian leader Vladimir Putin during a secret visit to Moscow. Axios reports this, citing two informed sources, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Ratcliffe raised the possibility of resuming negotiations between Ukraine and the Russian Federation with U.S. mediation. His trip was partly intended to determine whether the heads of Russia’s intelligence services could influence Putin and persuade him to return to negotiations.
On Friday, U.S. officials briefed Zelenskyy on the results of Ratcliffe’s talks in Moscow and his proposal for a trilateral summit. Washington had already put forward such an idea earlier – Zelenskyy supported it, while Putin rejected it.
Ratcliffe attempted to revive the diplomatic process
During a secret trip to Moscow on Tuesday, the CIA director met with the head of the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service, Sergei Naryshkin, and FSB Director Alexander Bortnikov. According to Axios, after the talks Ratcliffe concluded that Bortnikov could help revive diplomatic efforts.
The US informed Ukraine about a series of meetings in Moscow - Zelenskyy28.08.26, 19:31 • 6182 views
At the same time, Ukrainian officials are skeptical about Putin’s readiness to reach agreements. According to their information, Russia’s leadership is instead considering scenarios involving further escalation and possible offensive actions in northern Ukraine.
The negotiating process mediated by the United States effectively stalled in mid-February. At the same time, Kyiv allows for contacts with the Russian side under U.S. mediation to resume as early as September.
Reminder
CIA Director John Ratcliffe secretly visited Moscow this week, where he met with FSB Director Alexander Bortnikov. During the meeting, the U.S. official conveyed to the Russian side a bleak assessment of Russia’s military and economic situation and urged the Kremlin to seriously consider the possibility of ending the war against Ukraine.

Senator Elizabeth Warren calls Trump ‘the most corrupt president ever in American history’
TEHRAN — US Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has delivered a scathing critique of President Donald Trump, labeling him "the most corrupt president ever in American history" and accusing major energy corporations aligned with his administration of reaping vast financial gains from the military conflict against Iran.
Speaking at an election campaign rally for a junior senator from Massachusetts, Warren emphasized that oil executives who poured millions into political campaigns are now extracting massive corporate windfall earnings as energy costs skyrocket for ordinary working families. She pointed out that the single fastest path to relieving energy burdens on everyday citizens is to halt military operations in the region immediately, declaring that ending the campaign in Iran would instantly lower fuel prices at home. “So the question becomes: What do we do about that? When Donald Trump starts a war with Iran and his oil buddies, who gave him a million dollars for his campaign—when they start making profits like crazy, then our job is to call it out and fight back. That’s what we do,” Warren told the roaring crowd during her address. “You want to lower the price of gasoline? End the war in Iran. Just end it,” she added, directly challenging the White House's foreign policy rationale.
The senator's blunt assessment comes alongside recent official financial disclosure filings showing that Trump continues to hold and actively trade stock portfolios in major natural gas and petroleum giants. While White House spokespersons maintain that these portfolio movements operate independently of presidential oversight, political analysts and watchdog organizations highlight the undeniable conflict of interest in overseeing a massive military operation while maintaining tens of millions of dollars in personal equity tied directly to energy conglomerates that profit from wartime market volatility.
Financial data analyzed by congressional committees reveals that major US oil corporations—including ExxonMobil and Chevron—have seen their quarterly earnings multiply dramatically since the outbreak of hostilities, with corporate profits topping tens of billions of dollars and driving executive net worth to historic highs. Senate Joint Economic Committee reports indicate that Trump's personal energy portfolio alone has surged in value by over $15 million during the conflict, growing by an average of nearly 40 percent since the beginning of the year. Inside the US Congress, a steadily growing coalition of anti-war lawmakers and progressive representatives has voiced fierce opposition to the administration's aggressive policy in West Asia, strongly condemning the unprovoked and illegal nature of the military actions.
Opponents in Capitol Hill argue that the executive branch deliberately bypassed constitutional war powers requirements to embark on a disastrous military campaign that severely jeopardizes international stability, harms America's standing on the global stage, and serves narrow corporate interests over the welfare of the American public. Members of Congress are demanding an immediate cessation of offensive military funding and an end to weapon transfers, asserting that hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars currently being spent on overseas military interventions must instead be redirected toward fixing crumbling domestic infrastructure, expanding healthcare access, and alleviating the severe economic burdens faced by working families at home.
The broader international crisis stems from the joint military operations initiated by US and Israeli forces against Iran on February 28, targeting military sites and civil infrastructure, including residential area. Iranian defense forces responded under international frameworks of self-defense as recognized by Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, deploying advanced missile capabilities and maritime operational measures to neutralize hostile targets, protect territorial integrity, and assert strict defensive control over critical strategic transit corridors such as the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has repeatedly affirmed its right to defend its territory against foreign hostility, maintaining that regional security must be governed by regional nations without imperialist interference.
Six months into the military campaign, the US armed forces face operational constraints, highlighted by the rapid depletion of critical precision-guided munition stockpiles, Patriot interceptors, and complex air defense systems. US defense industrial supply chains continue to struggle under severe structural bottlenecks and material shortages, rendering the rapid replenishment of key military hardware functionally impossible in the short term. At the same time, the broader American domestic economy suffers from persistent inflation, soaring pump prices, rising shipping fees, and expanding public debt, leaving working-class citizens to bear the financial costs of an overextended foreign policy. Public dissatisfaction across major cities continues to surge as critics point out the glaring contrast between unlimited funding for foreign military actions and the neglected needs of the domestic population.

articles.title: The Third World War may be fought with weapons built in garages
articles.body:
The Third World War may be fought with weapons built in garages
“And out of the smoke locusts came down on the earth and were given power like that of scorpions of the earth…” – Revelation 9:3-5.
NATO has reportedly drawn up a plan for war with Russia in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states. At first glance, the document might seem unremarkable given the most senior officer involved in preparing it holds the rank of major, because every year, Russian and American military academies produce hundreds of officers capable of writing plans of this sort.
But two things make it worth paying attention to. The first is that modern military science is undergoing a profound crisis and the old methods of warfare are becoming increasingly difficult to use. Tank breakthroughs, deep encirclements and prolonged artillery barrages are all far more dangerous than they were even a decade ago because the battlefield is saturated with unmanned aerial vehicles.
The second is more surprising as military plans for a potential war aren’t usually made public, therefore NATO appears to be sending a message that we understand how warfare has changed, and we’re preparing for it.
The outlines of a possible non-nuclear Third World War can already be seen in such planning, but that assumes, of course, that nuclear powers could become involved in a global confrontation without crossing the nuclear threshold, instead fighting through local allies and proxies. What stands out in the NATO concept is the central role given to robotic and autonomous systems.
Fully autonomous warfare still belongs partly to the future, but even remotely controlled systems have already changed tactics more dramatically than almost any military innovation of the modern era. The closest historical comparison may be the arrival of rifled weapons, when massed column attacks became suicidal.
Only a few years ago, tanks were still regarded as the decisive instrument of land warfare, yet today a tank may struggle even to reach its firing position because the approaches are covered by drones, including so-called ‘waiters’ that land, remain concealed, and take off only when ordered to attack.
Technology has changed the battlefield with extraordinary speed and now NATO has published a defense concept for the three small Baltic states that appears to acknowledge this new reality. The importance of the document lies less in the rank of the officers who drafted it than in the fact that the alliance is publicly demonstrating its readiness for a different kind of war.I suspect that was the main reason for publishing it and the message is directed at an adversary that already has four years of intensive combat experience. The contours of a future non-nuclear world war are therefore becoming clearer. I’m not a military specialist, so I will speak only in broad terms. Human soldiers may increasingly be concentrated in elite formations and special forces, while much of the conventional battlefield is handed over to machines.
Back in the late 1980s, a special forces officer once told me that such units were becoming less useful when employed in support of large conventional armies and he predicted a gradual decline in the importance of elite formations, but history may now be turning in the opposite direction.
Perhaps the armies of the future will consist largely of small groups of highly trained soldiers operating in support of vast numbers of robotic systems. Drones have already transformed warfare and artificial intelligence and autonomous platforms may transform it far more radically.If that happens, enormous armies could become obsolete and inflicting strategic damage on an enemy may no longer require columns of armored vehicles or millions of soldiers. Nor would it necessarily require the gigantic defense-industrial complexes familiar from the 20th century as much of the equipment could be cheap and rapidly replaceable.
Even today, effective drones can be assembled in a garage, but of course, future combat systems will require increasingly sophisticated electronics, although it’s not yet clear how different many of those components will be from technologies already used in smartphones and consumer electronics.
This would also change the nature of military targets, for why attack an enemy’s tanks if you can disable the electricity that allows its entire military system to function?
Power stations will inevitably become heavily protected, but transmission networks are much more difficult to defend and it’s impossible to guard every kilometer of high-voltage cable. This could lead to a new emphasis on dispersed electricity generation and the Soviet Union already experimented with unconventional solutions in remote northern regions, including the use of nuclear technology originally developed for submarines. The economics of war would change as well given that drones are operated by small teams – or eventually by autonomous systems – and are cheap compared to the industrial machinery of traditional warfare.
 They also reduce the enormous logistical burden associated with artillery, where a shell must be manufactured, transported by rail, moved again by truck and finally delivered to a gun. Even then, dozens or hundreds may need to be fired to destroy a single target. The scale of traditional warfare is difficult to comprehend. During one offensive in the First World War, the Entente fired roughly 25 million artillery shells, while the Central Powers mobilized about the same number of men over the entire conflict.
Modern precision weapons are far more effective, but they are also increasingly expensive, and massed artillery itself is becoming vulnerable to drones and counter-battery systems. That’s why the Third World War, if it comes, may look nothing like the previous two.It may not begin with millions of soldiers crossing borders or vast tank armies moving across Europe. Instead, it could consist of many simultaneous regional conflicts fought by smaller allies of nuclear powers, while the great powers themselves remain protected beneath their nuclear umbrellas.
A future world war may therefore not be one enormous battlefield but dozens of smaller ones, connected by drones, satellites, artificial intelligence, and the political interests of states that can’t afford to fight one another directly.
This article was first published by Gazeta.ru, translated and edited by RT team

In response, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities, and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV.
A spokesperson said the US would pay for the attack economically and militarily, according to the semi-official news agency Fars.
Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported the US attack was a drone strike.
On Sunday night, Reuters reported a US source as saying that all incoming missiles on US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact so far.
The exchange of strikes came shortly after the US-Iran war hit the six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.
The US said its attacks were aimed at preventing Iran from launching more sea mines into the strait, days after it announced it had completed clearing explosives from the strategic waterway.
Donald Trump said last week that all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait of Hormuz and Iran had been told that any ship or boat placing new mines would be destroyed.
The last known US strikes on Iran were in late July and the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks, with Washington threatening to impose costly sanctions on countries that support Iran.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. The Iran war has now crossed its six-month mark.
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war to no avail.
While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming and Washington has since declared “economic warfare” against Tehran.
US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions. Eighteen US service members have been killed in the conflict.
The war has led to the blockade of the strait of Hormuz, which before the conflict accounted for the transit of about a fifth of the world’s oil barrels consumed.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Documents leaked by Trump official to bolster a conspiracy show ‘absolutely nothing’
articles.body:
A botched leak of purportedly explosive government files to a prominent conservative online personality was supposed to offer proof of what the Trump administration and its allies have long alleged: that a little-known office inside the US state department, created to fight foreign propaganda, had secretly become a tool for domestic censorship.
Two former high-ranking officials at the Global Engagement Center (GEC), a target of Republican ire that lost its funding in 2024 and was disbanded after Donald Trump’s return to office in 2025, say the documents show nothing of the kind.
Instead, they argue, the files are a symptom of a protracted and bitter political fight over an office that spent nearly a decade tracking and countering foreign influence operations, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.
And the state department is now resuming some of this work in other parts of its operation, including plans – laid out in a proposal reviewed by the Guardian – to pay social media influencers across south-east Asia as part of an $11m campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.
Sarah Rogers, the state department’s undersecretary for public diplomacy, provided the so-called “GEC files” to Jennica Pounds, a rightwing online data analyst known as DataRepublican – only for Pounds to claim earlier this month she was leaked the documents as part of a bid to “entrap” her.
Rogers, who denied this claim, then published the files herself, claiming officials inside the center “betrayed their stated mission”. The files included a 2022 GEC report on “gendered disinformation”, a flashpoint in the culture wars.
“These guys have consistently misrepresented what the GEC did, and this was a great example of that,” said Daniel Kimmage, who served as the center’s principal deputy coordinator and acting coordinator from its founding in 2017 until its complete dissolution in 2025. His own congressional testimony was included in the leaked files.
Kimmage and Carrie Goux, a Joe Biden appointee and the center’s former acting deputy coordinator, say nothing in the material shows the GEC, whose mandate was explicitly foreign-facing, ever turned its tools on Americans.
“If the smoking gun was a gendered disinformation report, that feels like they came up short,” Goux said. “There seems to be absolutely nothing here.”
Weaponization
The dispute is the latest chapter in a years-long campaign by conservatives to portray the GEC as part of a broader effort by the US government and technology companies to suppress rightwing speech.
Republican congressmen including Michael McCaul, former chair of the House foreign affairs committee, argued in a July 2024 letter that the GEC was “at best indifferent to, and at worst complicit in” stretching the definition of disinformation to “censor” conservative speech in the US.
Trump’s return to the presidency drew this view into the heart of the federal government. The center was abolished in 2025, and what remained of its work scattered across the state department.
Much of that Republican-led campaign centered on how the GEC had funded the Global Disinformation Index (GDI), a UK-based non-profit that rates media outlets by how likely they are to spread disinformation, to help monitor propaganda in Asia. But in 2022 the GDI separately published its own study of the US media market that rated several conservative outlets, including Newsmax, One America News and the New York Post, as high-risk – a finding its critics have cited ever since as evidence that a foreign-facing office had funded a group meddling in domestic politics.
The question raised by the files leaked this month is narrower, however: whether they show the GEC itself ran a domestic censorship operation. Kimmage and Goux insist they do not.
Kimmage said his own congressional testimony, which Rogers included in the leak, had been selectively read. “If you look at the transcript, [the question was], ‘Does GEC take positions on US outlets?’ And I said, ‘No, it didn’t,’” he said.
Rogers “tried to twist that into something that it wasn’t”, according to Kimmage. “For people who talk a lot about weaponization of government, this seems a lot closer to the weaponization of government and psy-opping of the American people than anything that the emails from the Global Engagement Center show.”
‘False’ allegations
Pounds, the rightwing analyst, is not a neutral bystander. Days after the documents were released, she disclosed that she had been quietly working since July as a special government employee for the defense department.
On Friday, Pounds released a database to track US citizens in the Democratic Socialists of America. The Pentagon did not respond when asked whether the database is included in her scope of government work.
Both former senior officials, Kimmage and Goux, draw a sharp line between the accusations made by critics of the GEC and what the center actually did. “We were not ever looking at Americans,” Goux said. “We were looking at the foreign actors and what their [tactics, techniques and procedures] … are doing overseas.”
The GEC “did what its congressional mandate charged it to do, which is to fight foreign [misinformation and] disinformation”, added Kimmage. “This allegation that it’s censoring Americans is false.”
During its almost decade-long existence, the center published eight detailed public reports on Russian and Chinese information operations and ran four major exposures of Russian disinformation campaigns – in Latin America, Africa and Moldova, and on the Kremlin-linked network RT.
Its largest such operation traced a Kremlin-backed effort called the “African Initiative”, which the center said had recruited local journalists, bloggers and public figures to spread conspiracy theories about US-funded health programs across the continent.
In January 2024, the GEC helped broker an international pact on countering foreign state disinformation that eventually drew more than two dozen government signatories, among them Moldova, Spain, Estonia, Poland and Finland – a framework its backers hoped other countries would use to build their own version of the office.
A 2022 inspector general review found the GEC “generally effective” at supporting counter-disinformation programs overall, while flagging weaknesses in its internal controls, contractor oversight and strategic planning. That record was enough to sustain bipartisan support: senators Rob Portman, a Republican, and Chris Murphy, a Democrat, repeatedly pushed to fund and strengthen the center, and its authorization survived multiple renewal fights before House Republicans, increasingly focused on the domestic-speech question, declined to extend it again in 2024.
That mandate cost roughly $61m per year. The GEC employed about 120 people before Congress declined to reauthorize it, letting the office lapse at the end of 2024. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, later folded what remained of its work into a new counter foreign information manipulation and interference office, framing the closure as an end to wasteful, censorious government overreach.
Trust exercise
Now, less than a year after the GEC shut down, a proposal reviewed by the Guardian shows the state department preparing to pay up to 30 online influencers across 11 countries in south-east Asia $2,500 apiece as part of an $11m, multi-year campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.
The project, which would be operated by the US Mission to USEAN, has three parts: a $5m messaging campaign, a $3m program training influencers and journalists to counter Chinese propaganda, and a $3m trip bringing about 180 participants to studios in Washington and Houston “for intensive collaboration, studio production and first-hand engagement with US institutions and creators”.
The proposal’s planning materials describe the ideal recruit as starting from a “welcoming” position of what one document calls the “rejecting-affirming continuum”: someone not yet sold on the US, but not hostile either. As participants move through the accelerator, the materials say, exposure to evidence of US commitment in the region and training in spotting propaganda from China (which has reportedly invested billions of dollars in disinformation efforts globally) is meant to carry them toward the “affirming” end of that scale, publicly backing closer ties with Washington on trade, tech standards and the South China Sea.
The document cited the rightwing analyst and new Pentagon special government employee, Jennica Pounds, the DataRepublican, as an ideal model to seek out in other recruits abroad.
Contacted for comment, the state department declined to directly address questions about the documents released by Rogers, the influencer proposal, the department’s current foreign influence programs and whether other regions are being targeted as well.
A state department official said: “Undersecretary Rogers has been clear that the department will continue to confront censorship, anti-American propaganda and coercive influence directly while demonstrating the enduring advantages of freedom, accountability and open communication.”
Meanwhile, the office of policy, planning and resources for public diplomacy (R/PPR) was separately shopping for commercial help with a similar mission this spring. A government filing from May 2026 shows the R/PPR requesting information from vendors on software that can mine open-source data, map “adversarial propaganda influence networks” and detect deepfakes.
That apparent contradiction is not lost on the GEC’s former staff.
“Are they trying to re-create it? Probably,” Goux said. “But now they’re spending a lot more tax dollars doing that, trying to get contractors to do some of the stuff that we were doing.”
Goux put the broader cost in plainer terms still. “The US has lost their seat at the table to do that, and that’s unfortunate,” she said. “I hope we can gain it back, but we’re losing trust too, and that’s significant.”

articles.title: Russian strike on Kyiv ammunition depot kills 38
articles.body:
The death toll from a Russian strike on an ammunition depot in Ukraine’s Kyiv region has risen to 38, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday, as rescue teams continued searching for four missing people and investigators examined the storage of explosives near residential areas.
The strike hit a military facility in Myla, west of Kyiv, late on Friday and triggered secondary explosions involving artillery shells, mines, drones and other munitions.
Zelenskyy said most fires had been extinguished, though emergency teams were still working through debris and contamination at the site.
Reuters reported that the attack was the deadliest Russian strike in the Kyiv region this year.
Dozens of people were injured and hundreds were evacuated from surrounding areas. At least 50 residential buildings and a care facility for elderly and disabled people were damaged, while regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said 42 people, including four children, were injured.
The incident has also prompted a criminal investigation into the storage of ammunition close to civilian buildings.
“There are regulations in place; ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas,” Zelenskyy said.
He described the situation as “terrible negligence” and said criminal proceedings had been opened against officials responsible for the storage arrangements.
Among those killed was Taras Didych, head of the Dmytrivka community, who died while helping others after the attack, Zelenskyy said.
The blast follows another strike-related detonation at an ammunition site in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, in July. Ukrainian officials said that incident had already exposed failures in the storage of explosives near residential areas.
Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said authorities had failed to learn from the earlier case.
“In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence,” he said on Telegram.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had targeted a depot in Myla storing components and launch boosters for Ukrainian long-range drones.
The strike formed part of a wider Russian air campaign against Kyiv and other regions. Zelenskyy said Russia had launched nearly 2,000 attack drones, more than 1,600 aerial bombs and 31 missiles against Ukraine over the previous week.
Separate Russian attacks also killed civilians in Kyiv and the Boryspil district on Saturday, according to Ukrainian officials.
HT

articles.title: Ukrainian drones destroy Russian air defense, radar systems at Yeysk, Millerovo airfields
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones destroy Russian air defense, radar systems at Yeysk, Millerovo airfields
Ukraine conducted overnight long-range strikes on Russian military infrastructure, destroying air defense and radar systems at two military airfields, Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert "Madyar" Brovdi said Aug. 30.
Madyar said Ukrainian drones targeted the Yeysk airfield in Russia's Krasnodar Krai and the Millerovo airfield in Rostov Oblast.
According to Madyar, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense system, a Sopka-2 radar, and an aviation weapons depot at the Yeysk airfield. They also destroyed Kasta 2E2, RSP-27, and Nebo-SV radar systems, as well as aviation facilities and a depot at the Millerovo airfield, he said.
The destruction of the Russian air defense and radar systems was confirmed by additional reconnaissance, Madyar said.
He said the main target of the operation was a DRL-27 module of Russia's RSP-27 aircraft landing radar system at Millerovo. The radar is used both to detect aerial targets and to control air traffic at the airfield, working together with a PRL-27 landing radar.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.
The strikes are part of Ukraine's intensifying campaign against the Russian military and energy infrastructure. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Aug. 28 that Ukraine should significantly increase the frequency of its long-range drone strikes against Russia, setting a goal of launching 1,000 such drones a day.
Ukraine currently launches more than 300 long-range drones on average each day, Zelensky said, arguing that the number needs to rise as Russia intensifies its aerial attacks against Ukrainian cities.
Ukraine has increasingly used long-range drones to strike Russian military and energy infrastructure far behind the front line, while Russia continues to launch large-scale drone and missile attacks against Ukrainian cities.

articles.title: War update: 221 clashes along front line over past day, fiercest fighting in Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka sectors

articles.title: Greece to sign $3.6b. Israeli air defense deal, creating 'Achilles Shield' against Turkey and Iran
articles.body:
Greece is set to sign a $3.6 billion defense deal with Israel on Monday in Tel Aviv, a major agreement that will provide Athens with a multilayered air defense system against potential threats from Turkey and Iran.
The agreement, negotiated over three years, will become the largest defense export deal in Israel’s history.
A Greek delegation will sign the agreement with Israel’s Defense Ministry to purchase air defense systems valued at $3.6 billion, slightly below earlier estimates. The deal will provide Greece, for the first time, with an integrated, multilayered defense network.
Most of the funds will go to Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, which will supply Greece with David’s Sling systems designed to intercept heavy rockets and ballistic missiles, as well as mobile SPYDER systems designed to counter unmanned aerial vehicles and drones.
Israel Aerospace Industries will provide the Barak MX system, which is designed to defend against aircraft and missiles.
Project 'Achilles Shield'
The agreement also includes a national-level command-and-control center to operate the systems and manage launches, similar to the system used in Israel. The center will incorporate artificial intelligence capabilities.
Greek companies are expected to receive about €700 million of the deal’s total value as subcontractors for Rafael and IAI.
The project is known in Greece as “Achilles Shield” and will include deploying SPYDER batteries on Greek islands, including popular vacation destinations visited by many Israelis.
The largest defense export deal in Israel’s history to date was IAI’s first export sale of the Arrow 3 missile defense system to Germany, worth $3.5 billion, signed in 2023.
Greece is already a major Israeli customer
Elbit Systems announced a $2.3 b. deal with a foreign customer this year, according to reports from the Persian Gulf, while Rafael signed a framework agreement with Romania this year to sell SPYDER systems worth $2 b.
Greece has already become a major customer of Israel’s defense industry, purchasing Spike missiles and SPICE precision-guided bombs from Rafael, Rampage missiles from Elbit Systems and IAI, and Heron 2 drones from IAI.
The air defense agreement is expected to further strengthen the strategic partnership between the two countries, with Israel playing a key role in helping protect Greek airspace.
Greece, Cyprus, and Israel have strengthened their security coordination in recent years amid growing tensions with Turkey.
Cyprus has also reportedly purchased Israel’s Barak MX system to defend its airspace, according to foreign reports.

articles.title: Turkey, Saudi, Pakistan to hold first defence pact meeting
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan to hold first defence pact meeting
Top officials from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will gather in Istanbul on Monday for a first committee meeting under the defence pact they signed this month, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
The "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement", signed on 7 August, brought together Sunni Muslim US allies concerned by the Iran war and regional conflict that has led to Iranian missile fire on Gulf oil exporters.
It is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack on all, similar to NATO's Article 5 collective defence clause.
Foreign and defence ministers, as well as the chiefs of staff, of the three countries will attend the meeting in Istanbul, the ministry source said.
"International security issues will be on the agenda," the source said, with discussions expected to cover enhancing defence capabilities, greater interoperability among their armed forces and deepening cooperation in the defence industry, including joint production and development.
The three nations share concerns about the military stances of Israel and revolutionary Shi'ite Iran, as long-time ally the US struggles to contain regional upheaval that has caused a global energy crisis.
Six months after the US and Israel launched the war against Iran, negotiations are at an impasse and President Donald Trump's administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an "economic D-Day".
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest military, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion - with Egypt as a potential candidate - and did not seek to replace existing alliances.
(Reuters)

articles.title: Over 242,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine identified by media investigation
articles.body:
Russian independent media outlet Mediazona, in collaboration with the BBC Russian service, has confirmed the identities of 242,747 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine.
Since the media outlets' last update in mid-August, the names of 3,393 Russian soldiers have been added to the list of casualties. The latest count covers confirmed military deaths from Feb. 24, 2022, through Aug. 27, 2026.
The journalists note that the actual figures are likely significantly higher, as their verified information comes from public sources such as obituaries, posts by relatives, regional media reports, and statements from local authorities.
The confirmed death toll now includes over 88,600 volunteers, 26,600 recruited prisoners, and 20,000 mobilized soldiers, according to the media outlets. A total of 7,596 officers have also been confirmed to have been killed.
According to the outlets, the date of death is known in 225,000 cases, accounting for nearly 93% of confirmed casualties.
The Kyiv Independent cannot independently verify the reporting.
While casualty estimates have varied, independent Western assessments have consistently concluded that Russian losses significantly exceed Ukrainian casualties.
On July 31, President Volodymyr Zelensky disclosed estimates revealing that Russian forces had suffered around 1.6 million military casualties since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, including approximately 700,000 killed.
Zelensky added that around 50,000 Ukrainian service members had been killed and approximately 400,000 wounded.
The General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces estimates that as of Aug. 30, Russia has lost around 1,486,600 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 22, 2022. The figures do not specify killed or wounded, though the overall consensus is that it includes dead, wounded, missing, and captured.
According to Western intelligence, throughout 2026, Russia's Armed Forces has fallen short of reaching its recruitment target of 30,000 soldiers per month, losing more soldiers than they are recruiting on a monthly bases — leading the Kremlin to consider additional rounds of mobilization.
Ukraine's President's Office said on Aug. 27 that Russia plans to mobilize 600,000 recruits in 2026-27 as growing public dissatisfaction with the war in Ukraine reduces the number of people willing to volunteer.
Meanwhile Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov warned on Aug. 28 that Ukraine cannot afford to mobilize less than 30,000 people per month, as ending the war in the short term is "unrealistic."
As Mediazona continues to compile and maintain a list of Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine since the start of the full-scale war, the Kremlin added Mediazona to its "foreign agents" list for a second time, the outlet reported on Aug. 21.

articles.title: NATO driving the Arctic toward ‘militarization’ – Lavrov (FULL ARTICLE)
articles.body:
NATO driving the Arctic toward ‘militarization’ – Lavrov (FULL ARTICLE)
NATO is driving the militarization of the Arctic through intense military preparations that pose a direct threat to Russia’s security and increase the risk of direct armed confrontation, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
However, other than the members of the US-led military bloc, the overwhelming majority of countries are willing to engage with Moscow on equal and mutually beneficial terms, the top diplomat wrote in an article for Arctic.ru published on Monday.
The sweeping article touched on Moscow’s plans to develop Arctic shipping and maritime logistics along its Northern Sea Route, upcoming international cooperation, and the steady erosion of previous guardrails for multilateral collaboration in the region.
Read the full text below:
On August 19, a landmark event took place in Arctic shipping. For the first time, a container ship from China arrived at the port of Murmansk via the Northern Sea Route, a vital part of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor. In collaboration with our international partners, this represents the start of a new phase in the development of Russia’s Arctic region, which accounts for at least 10% of the country’s GDP and is home to more than 2.5 million of our citizens. In this regard, I would like to share a number of considerations on how we assess the current state of affairs in the Arctic and how we plan to develop international cooperation there.
Russia and international partners in the Arctic
The Foundations of the Russian State Policy in the Arctic for the Period up to 2035, approved by President Vladimir Putin, focus the efforts of all government bodies on improving the quality of life for the population of the Arctic zone of the Russian Federation, promoting economic growth in its territories, protecting the environment, and fostering mutually beneficial international cooperation. The latter is of particular importance to the Foreign Ministry, which is entrusted with coordinating functions in relations with foreign countries and intergovernmental organizations. And, I would like to emphasize, the whole range of issues relating to the development of the Arctic zone, maritime logistics and the Northern Sea Route plays an important role in the activities of the Maritime Board of the Russian Federation.
Foreign policy priorities at high latitudes have been enshrined in the currently effective Concept of the Foreign Policy of the Russian Federation of March 31, 2023. In the Arctic, Russia is seeking to preserve peace and stability, reduce the level of threats to national security, and create favorable external conditions for the country’s socio-economic development. We are open to interaction with all constructively minded foreign countries displaying reciprocal readiness to put these ideas into practice. There are quite a few such countries. The vast resource, transport, and logistics potential of the Far North, its unique natural and climatic features, long-standing traditions of regional cooperation, and the rich cultural heritage of its indigenous peoples offer broad opportunities for advantageous partnership.
The countries that cooperate closely with us in the Arctic include, first and foremost, China and India. Substantive discussions on Arctic issues take place with Beijing during regular meetings between the heads of government. The specialized bilateral sub-commission on the Northern Sea Route is operational, as are mechanisms for interministerial consultations and scientific exchanges. The results speak for themselves: they include the launch of regular container shipments across Russia’s northern seas, with plans to increase their frequency, and other achievements, including in polar research.
We are engaged in an active dialogue with New Delhi on issues related to high latitudes. In late August, it was discussed at a meeting of the Russian-Indian Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technical, and Cultural Cooperation. Indian corporations are involved in developing the resource potential of Russia’s Arctic region. According to some experts, the Arctic could become a major area of cooperation between Russia and India over the next 20 years.
There are prospects for interaction in the Far North with Brazil, Indonesia, Iran and other BRICS countries. We are also ready to develop cooperation with Belarus and other partners and allies in the CIS. South Korea and Singapore should also be mentioned as showing an interest in joint work with Russia in some Arctic projects, notwithstanding their participation in the unfriendly sanction campaign launched by the collective West against our country.
The interest of non-Arctic countries in establishing cooperation with Russia in the High North is reflected in the active participation of foreign guests in symposia and conferences devoted to Arctic issues. Numerous foreign delegations will take part in discussions during special sessions at the 11th Eastern Economic Forum, which opens on September 1 in Vladivostok. Next March, we look forward to welcoming distinguished guests from abroad to the next major international forum of the Russian Arctic, The Arctic – Territory of Dialogue, which will take place in Murmansk.
Challenges affecting international cooperation in the Arctic
Preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation meets the interests of the entire international community, and Russia is undoubtedly interested in this as well. However, there are those who do not share this point of view. How else can one explain the fact that NATO countries, as well as the Alliance as a whole, are driving the region towards militarization and creating hotbeds of international tension there?
In February 2026, NATO launched its Arctic Sentry operation, designed to expand its military presence in the High North. Intensive military preparations are underway in close proximity to our northern borders. NATO is conducting large-scale military exercises involving non-regional countries and introducing new components of its command-and-control system.
Such military activity in the Far North poses a direct threat to Russia’s security. It also increases the risk of incidents that could trigger an armed confrontation with potentially disastrous consequences.
This deliberate and systematic effort to foster an atmosphere of mistrust in the military sphere is taking place alongside Western attempts to undermine Russia’s legitimate rights in international cooperation through illegitimate financial and economic sanctions targeting legal entities and individuals from countries of the Global Majority involved in joint projects in the Arctic region.
NATO members and other Western countries make no secret of their true motives, openly declaring their intention to turn the Arctic into a new front for opposing the development of Russia and its like-minded partners.
One manifestation of the West’s anti-Russian policy has been the disruption of previously effective mechanisms of multilateral cooperation in the Far North. Some have ceased to exist altogether, while others have largely lost their relevance without Russia’s participation, after Moscow was forced to suspend its engagement with them in response to hostile actions. The Arctic Council, established almost 30 years ago, on September 19, 1996, remains the only functioning intergovernmental organization.
The Council is approaching its anniversary in a shape that is far from ideal. Since March 2022, as a result of actions by its Western member states, its work has effectively been frozen, leaving the organization in a severe crisis. Ministerial meetings and sessions of its key coordinating body, the Senior Arctic Officials, have been suspended, while its capacity to implement projects has been significantly curtailed. The Council’s activities are now largely confined to expert-level contacts and remote meetings of its working bodies.
Russia is ready to resume the full-fledged work of the Arctic Council, provided that all parties engage in good faith and take into account the legitimate interests of every participant. At the same time, we are prepared for the scenario currently being pursued by NATO countries within the organization as they attempt to discuss Arctic issues among themselves, without Russia, thereby effectively discrediting and marginalizing the Arctic Council. Should this scenario materialize, Russia has the territory, logistics, technology, and reliable partners needed to carry out mutually beneficial projects and confidently implement its plans in the Arctic.
The future of international cooperation in the Arctic
A glance at the world map makes it clear that Russia has been, is, and will remain a leading Arctic state. As climate change continues and the polar ice cover recedes, experts predict that the Arctic will become increasingly accessible for transportation and resource development. The region is already playing an increasingly important role in maintaining stable trade links amid more frequent disruptions to global supply chains, particularly in the straits of the world’s oceans that are of systemic importance to the global economy.
The strategic importance of the Arctic to our country’s national interests and security will also continue to grow. We will pursue the comprehensive development of the High North and further expand the infrastructure of Russia’s Arctic zone in accordance with Russian law and the country’s development priorities.
In our economic activities, we will continue to proceed from the understanding that the Arctic maritime areas form an integral part of the World Ocean. The provisions of the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which establish special rights and responsibilities for coastal states in the Arctic, apply there in full. Commitment to these rights and responsibilities was reaffirmed in the Ilulissat Declaration, adopted in 2008 by the five Arctic coastal states – Russia, Denmark, Canada, Norway, and the United States. At this stage, we see no need to develop new international legal instruments governing economic and other activities in the High North.
Russia’s foreign policy in the Arctic will remain comprehensive and pragmatic. We support the Arctic’s development as an integral part of the broader Eurasian space of security and cooperation.
Our current opponents should have learned the many lessons of history by now and understood that attempts to speak to Russia in the language of sanctions and threats are futile. Unfriendly and hostile actions have been and will continue to be met with an appropriate response, including asymmetric measures. Russia favors constructive dialogue in all regions of the world, but, when necessary, we will defend our national interests by all available means.
As President of Russia Vladimir Putin has repeatedly emphasized, extensive work is underway in the Arctic, and we are open to cooperation with all partners willing to engage on the basis of equality and mutual benefit. Such partners, beyond the circle of NATO countries pursuing Russophobic policies, constitute the overwhelming majority.Promising areas of cooperation include the development of natural resources and the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor, including its key component, the Northern Sea Route. Priorities also include the development of industrial, transport, and tourism infrastructure.Improving the well-being of people living in the Far North, preserving the Arctic environment, and advancing scientific research will also remain key priorities. In all these areas, we see international cooperation as playing a major role.

articles.title: Ukrainian General Staff reports strikes on Kirishi oil refinery and Yeysk airfield in Russia
articles.body:
Ukrainian General Staff reports strikes on Kirishi oil refinery and Yeysk airfield in Russia
Ukraine's defence forces struck the Kirishi oil refinery in Russia's Leningrad Oblast and the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar Krai on the night of 29-30 August.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine; Ukraine's Special Operations Forces
Details: A fire was reported at the Kirishi oil refinery following the strike.
The Special Operations Forces said they carried out the operation together with the Security Service of Ukraine, the Unmanned Systems Forces and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
The General Staff said the refinery is Russia's second-largest by capacity and the largest in the country's north-west. It has an annual processing capacity of around 20 million tonnes of oil.
The facility produces motor fuel, aviation fuel and diesel and, according to Ukraine's General Staff, supplies Russian troops.
The military airfield in Yeysk was also struck, with a fire reported at the site.
In addition, a facility for storing, preparing and launching attack drones was struck in Millerovo, Rostov Oblast. A fire was also reported there.
The extent of the damage is being assessed.
Background: Russian authorities in Leningrad Oblast previously reported an attack by more than 60 drones and a strike on the Kirishi oil refinery.

articles.title: US forces strike Iranian launchers on Larak island in Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
US forces strike Iranian launchers on Larak island in Strait of Hormuz
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in the first military action in a month, a US official said Sunday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the US attack on Larak island killed and wounded several Iranian fighters and civilians, and vowed to punish those responsible.
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in the first military action in a month on Sunday, according to a US official, breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months.
Forces with the Revolutionary Guard Corps were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military movements.
The US military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
Semiofficial news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak island on the strait. The Guard in a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster noted “the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots.”
The statement said the attack will “result in punishment of the aggressor.”
The fighting comes just days after the Trump administration said it would turn its focus to increasing economic pressure — rather than military action — to try to end its war with Iran. The shifting strategy centers on threats to punish any country or entity that continues to conduct business with Tehran.
The turn to using sanctions as the cudgel of choice comes as the administration weighs diminished munitions stockpiles after months of war, sparking concerns that the prolonged conflict could undermine US military readiness in other parts of the globe.
Read moreTrump says Strait of Hormuz demined, warns of ‘zero tolerance’ for new mines
As the conflict grinds on, Trump’s talk of finding a quick end to the war also appears to be fading. He stressed last week that he’s “not in a hurry” to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he continues making the case that the Islamic Republic’s leadership is on the ropes.
Appointments to Iran’s senior security leadership in the past month, however, have signaled Tehran’s defiance after weathering decades of sanctions as well as a lack of tolerance for dissent at home.
Trump has consistently emphasised that the US and Israel campaign has been devastating for Iran’s navy and air force. Iranian officials have said the country has suffered $270 billion in direct and indirect damage. Israeli military strikes in the first weeks of the war wiped out much of the theocratic government’s leadership structure.
But Iran has found leverage through its own strikes in the critical Strait of Hormuz where relatively few vessels carrying oil and liquefied natural gas are risking passage. Iran still has enough drones and missiles to fire at vessels transiting the vital energy waterway, through which 20% of the world's oil normally flows, effectively controlling much of the traffic in the strait.
Tehran continues to assert that even after it works out a management plan for the strait with Oman, its neighbor on the other side of the waterway, the US can't use it until it fulfills its obligations under the memorandum of understanding the countries signed in mid-June.
Trump has repeatedly declared that the “Strait of Hormuz is open,” saying 24 vessels passed through last week. But that’s a fraction of the roughly 130 vessels that transited daily before the war began.
Earlier on Sunday, a multinational coalition overseen by the US Navy said commercial traffic through the strait remained at “reduced levels.”
And a monitoring agency run by the British military said an unknown projectile struck a tanker ship on Saturday north of Khasab, Oman, in the strait. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organisation said no casualties or environmental impact had been reported, and cited unspecified military authorities. There was no immediate claim of responsibility.
The US military said that as of Sunday, it had redirected 83 commercial vessels and disabled three under its blockade of Iranian ports.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

articles.title: US seriously considers use of nuclear weapons in Europe
articles.body:
US military strategists are seriously considering the possibility of using nuclear weapons in Europe, Russian Foreign Ministry special envoy Andrey Belousov said in an interview with RT.
According to the diplomat, Washington’s efforts to initiate discussions on Russia’s non-strategic nuclear weapons serve to divert international attention from what he described as the threat posed by US nuclear weapons stationed in Europe, as well as Washington’s nuclear missile programs and plans.
"Speaking of this danger, it is impossible not to note that Washington’s insistence on initiating discussions at various multilateral disarmament forums on Russian non-strategic nuclear weapons, which do not threaten US territory, suggests that American military strategists are seriously considering the possibility of using nuclear weapons in the European theater of military operations," he said.
"Obtaining objective data on Russian non-strategic nuclear weapons through negotiations or discussions on strategic stability, the introduction of intrusive transparency measures, or their reduction - and especially their complete elimination - would increase the likelihood of a scenario involving the use of nuclear weapons by the US and its allies in Europe," Belousov added.
The diplomat stressed that European countries should recognize the full danger of what he described as Washington’s purely practical approach to the territory of its allies.
MNA

Russia’s Parliament Speaker Calls for Terror Against Ukrainian Civilians, Ukraine MFA Responds
Statements by Pyotr Tolstoy, deputy speaker of the Russian State Duma, regarding strikes on Ukrainian urban centers amount to public calls for war crimes, according to Heorhii Tykhyi, spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine.
The Ukrainian diplomatic representative emphasized that such declarations from Russian figures demand the creation of unlivable conditions for civilians. He added that these public comments warrant an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court.
