Ukrainian authorities and international bodies classify these strikes as deliberate war crimes committed by Russia. Systematic bombardment targeting life-support systems and medical facilities to deprive the population of electricity, heat, water, communications, and medical care constitutes evidence of genocidal actions.
Previously, in a phone conversation with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov announced that Russian forces were initiating systematic strikes on facilities in Kyiv.

articles.title: Trump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higher | Sina Toossi
articles.body:
Donald Trump has found a new way to promise victory over Iran. After months of war have failed to force Iran’s capitulation or collapse, his administration has unveiled what the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, calls Operation Economic Outcast: an effort to cut it off from what remains of the global economy and threaten foreign governments, banks and companies with sanctions if they continue doing business with Tehran.
There is no question that Iran is vulnerable. Its economy has been battered by years of sanctions, war and a months-long US naval blockade. Iranian officials acknowledge that oil exports and access to foreign currency have been severely constrained. Ordinary Iranians are already enduring high inflation, currency depreciation and worsening living standards. Further economic strangulation will inflict significant additional hardship.
Iran also wants an end to the war. Its president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has said it should seek peace while it can still negotiate from a position of “power and dignity”. But Iran needing a deal is not the same as Iran preparing to surrender. That distinction has repeatedly eluded Trump in formulating his Iran policy: ramping up pressure is not the same as having a strategy. Iran gets a move too.
Indeed, Iranian officials increasingly suggest this strategy has the opposite effect than what was intended. Each successive escalation, in their telling, demonstrates why Iran relinquishing its remaining leverage would simply leave it vulnerable to the next round of US pressure. The emerging strategy therefore appears to combine bargaining with endurance: seek an agreement while demonstrating that it can withstand the pressure without capitulating or abandoning its core terms.
This is why recent Iranian rhetoric deserves more attention than it has received.
Mohsen Rezaei, the new head of Iran’s supreme national security council, has called participation in Washington’s economic campaign an “act of war”. He says Tehran will first try to persuade neighbouring states not to participate, but has threatened their interests if they do. He has even warned that Iran could prevent Gulf oil exports through routes designed to bypass Hormuz.
These statements should not simply be dismissed as declarations of defiance for an audience in Iran. They reflect a consistent strategic logic: Iran cannot defeat the US economically, but it can try to make the economic strangulation of Iran prohibitively expensive for Washington and the countries it needs to enforce it.
That could mean tightening pressure on Hormuz, threatening infrastructure that enables alternative oil-export routes or putting greater pressure on US interests across the region. None of this would help ordinary Iranians. Escalation would compound their suffering. But that is precisely why Washington should think beyond the first-order effects of its own actions.
There is another weakness in Trump’s plan. For Bessent’s threat to work, Washington must persuade or coerce much of the world into participating, especially China, the principal buyer of Iranian oil. Yet Beijing is moving in the opposite direction. It has ordered firms not to comply with US sanctions targeting Chinese buyers of Iranian oil, while its top court recently highlighted a ruling penalising a Singaporean company for complying with US sanctions. Beijing has now warned it will take “all necessary measures” if Chinese interests are targeted.
Washington therefore faces an uncomfortable choice: tolerate continued trade between Iran and China, its neighbours and other partners, or dramatically escalate coercion of the governments, banks and companies that keep those channels open. That risks multiplying the US’s economic confrontations at a moment when it needs international cooperation to isolate Tehran. Bessent acknowledged the danger when asked why Washington was not immediately imposing its most sweeping secondary sanctions. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he responded. That is quite an admission for an operation advertised as “economic D-day”.
With the midterms approaching, the White House has strong incentives to avoid another major escalation that could further disrupt Gulf energy flows and send fuel prices soaring. Tehran knows this. Its gamble is that it can endure and reroute enough commerce while imposing enough costs that Washington and its partners eventually prefer a settlement to continued confrontation.
That makes this a dangerous contest of endurance. Washington is betting Iran’s economy completely breaks first. Tehran is betting the US’s tolerance for the war and its mounting economic costs breaks first.
This has been the recurring flaw in Trump’s approach. In 2018, he left the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran, in an attempt to secure more favourable terms. Iran instead expanded its nuclear programme. Military conflict was supposed to force Tehran to accept US terms. Instead, the war expanded and Hormuz became a central source of Iranian leverage. Now intensified economic strangulation is supposed to accomplish what military power could not.
Unless Trump starts thinking several moves ahead, his latest attempt to force Iran into submission could leave the US with even higher energy prices, an even more confrontational adversary and yet another escalation it never counted on.
- 
  Sina Toossi is a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, where his work focuses on US-Iran relations, US policy toward the Middle East and nuclear issues

Ukraine Aims to Launch 1,000 Long-Range Drones Daily at Russian Targets
Ukraine is set to scale up its output of long-range aerial drones to 1,000 units per day, up from the current daily average of about 300 units.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy outlined this objective on August 28 following a meeting of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief's Staff, where officials discussed expanding air defenses and shielding the country from Russian strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
President Zelenskyy noted that long-range operations are disrupting economic stability and supply networks across Russia, cutting into domestic petrol reserves and export volumes.
Expanding long-range capabilities is designed to increase economic pressure on Russia if it chooses to prolong Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and decline peace talks.
Ukrainian officials also emphasized the need to accelerate the manufacturing of interceptor drones to counter jet-powered Shahed attack drones recently deployed in higher volumes.
Reuters reported in late August that Russian petrol production dropped to approximately 80,000 metric tons per day against an internal requirement of roughly 115,000 metric tons. The resulting shortfall led several regions across Russia to reintroduce restrictions on fuel sales.
Ukraine systematically targeted Russia's oil refineries, striking all 11 of the country's largest facilities to erode the Kremlin's financial foundation.

articles.title: Iran rebuilds defense-industrial capacity after recent conflicts:  Defense Ministry
articles.body:
Iran rebuilds defense-industrial capacity after recent conflicts: Defense Ministry
TEHRAN — Iran is moving to replenish strategic weapons stocks and expand its defense-industrial capacity following two recent conflicts, with the Ministry of Defense focusing on production resilience, indigenous technology and lessons learned from combat, Defense Ministry spokesman Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik said.
Speaking to IRNA, Talaei-Nik said the government had provided sustained support to the Armed Forces throughout the conflicts. The support covered weapons, ammunition, equipment and other military materiel while efforts were made to maintain essential civilian supplies.
Talaei-Nik said attacks had affected around 25 provinces to varying degrees. He described the confrontation as asymmetric, with Iran facing opponents possessing significantly greater military resources and access to regional logistical and operational support. Despite this disparity, he stated, Iran’s adversaries failed to achieve their objectives.
According to Talaei-Nik, Iran’s pre-war accumulation of strategic stocks of weapons, equipment and ammunition enabled the Armed Forces to sustain operations during the fighting. The consumption of those reserves has now created a requirement for replenishment.
The spokesman also highlighted the resilience of Iran’s defense-industrial supply chain. Around 9,300 companies are involved in the country’s defense-production network, he said, with knowledge-based and private-sector firms accounting for roughly two-thirds of the industrial base in areas including components, raw materials and subsystems.
This distributed production network, Talaei-Nik said, helped maintain output even after some defense facilities were damaged.
He added that production of some weapons, equipment and ammunition had more than doubled between the 12-day war and the subsequent conflict (Ramadan war).
Talaei-Nik said Iran’s defense industry is undergoing a technological expansion, particularly in ballistic and cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). He said that domestic capabilities in several fields have moved beyond reverse engineering towards independent design and production.
The ministry is now rebuilding and expanding its industrial capacity based on operational lessons from the recent conflicts, assessments of future threats and input from scientific and research institutions.
New weapons, equipment, technical capabilities and tactics have also been prepared for potential future contingencies, Talaei-Nik said, although details would remain undisclosed to preserve operational surprise.
He argued that one of the key lessons of the conflicts was a miscalculation by Iran’s adversaries regarding the country’s ability to withstand sustained military and economic pressure.
Talaei-Nik said Iran’s core defense doctrine remains centered on “both integrated and asymmetric defense,” while operational and tactical methods are adjusted in response to changes in the battlefield and regional security environment.
The approach integrated defensive objectives with offensive operational measures intended to prevent an adversary from gaining the initiative, he said. The spokesman also pointed to improvements in Iran’s air-defense capabilities, particularly systems designed to counter advanced UAV threats.
He added that Defense Ministry personnel fatalities during the longer “Ramadan war” were approximately half those recorded during the earlier 12-day conflict, attributing the reduction partly to improved defensive capabilities and lessons learned from previous combat.
Talaei-Nik said foreign demand for Iranian defense products had been increasing before the recent conflicts. However, he stressed that replenishing domestic military stocks is now the priority, with exports dependent on production surpluses.
The spokesman said Iran manufactures more than 1,000 types of weapons, equipment and ammunition and has achieved more than 90% self-sufficiency in defense production, according to the ministry’s assessment.
He also highlighted efforts to lower production costs, stating that some Iranian defense products cost between one and 20 times less to manufacture than comparable foreign systems.
For Iran’s defense establishment, the post-conflict priority is therefore twofold: restoring stocks consumed during combat while using battlefield experience to accelerate technological development, strengthen industrial resilience, and improve operational readiness for future contingencies.

articles.title: Ukraine Hammers Two Russian Airfields in One Night, Triggering Fires and Ammunition Blasts
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hammers Two Russian Airfields in One Night, Triggering Fires and Ammunition Blasts
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian military aviation sites overnight on August 30, hitting the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar Krai and a facility used to store, prepare and launch attack drones in Millerovo in the Rostov region, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed on August 30.
Fires were recorded at both locations following the strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
At Yeysk, footage published by the OSINT community Exilenova+ showed a large fire inside the military airfield as secondary explosions consistent with detonating ammunition could be heard.
NASA’s FIRMS satellite fire-monitoring system also detected a blaze at the facility at around 4:02 am local time. Satellite data indicated that the affected area extended from the aircraft parking section toward the runway.
A drone warning had been issued across the region at approximately 2:58 am, including for the city of Yeysk. The alert remained active until 5:33 am, lasting roughly three hours.
Ukraine’s General Staff subsequently confirmed that the Yeysk military airfield had been hit and that a fire broke out on the site.
The Russian military uses Yeysk to support aviation operations, including aircraft capable of launching missiles and guided aerial bombs against Ukraine.
The base also hosts Russia’s 859th Center for Combat Application and Retraining of Naval Aviation Flight Personnel, making it an important training and support facility for Russian naval aviation.
Another distinctive feature of Yeysk is its NITKA ground-based aviation training complex, which replicates an aircraft carrier’s flight deck and landing systems. Russian naval aviators use the facility to practice carrier takeoffs and landings without operating at sea.
Repeated Ukrainian attacks have made Yeysk increasingly vulnerable, and Russian forces do not appear to station combat aircraft there permanently. However, aircraft can still be temporarily redeployed to the base ahead of operations.
Ukraine simultaneously struck a Russian drone operations facility in Millerovo, roughly 170 kilometers, or 105 miles, from the front line.
The General Staff said the target was used for the storage, preparation, and launch of Russian attack UAVs. A fire was recorded following the strike.
NASA FIRMS detected a fire in the Millerovo area at approximately 3:33 am local time after drone warnings were issued shortly after midnight.
The Millerovo military airfield is associated with Russia’s 31st Fighter Aviation Regiment, which operates Su-30SM multirole fighters.
The site has repeatedly come under Ukrainian attack because of its proximity to Ukraine and its role in supporting Russian military aviation and drone operations.
Russian forces also use infrastructure in the area to store ammunition, house personnel and maintain fuel and lubricant supplies.
Rostov regional governor Yuri Slyusar acknowledged a drone attack on Millerovo but did not publicly mention the military facility or the fire there.
Previously, Ukrainian drones struck a Russian Nebo-U radar station at the Millerovo military airfield in Russia’s Rostov region, a facility used to launch Shahed drones and other UAVs against Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russia’s Refineries So Bad Moscow Is Now Importing Fuel for Its Warplanes
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russia’s Refineries So Bad Moscow Is Now Importing Fuel for Its Warplanes
Systematic Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries have sharply reduced the country’s aviation fuel production, forcing Moscow to import Jet A-1 from South Korea and Egypt to support both military and civilian aviation, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said on August 29.
According to HUR, Russia has also temporarily banned exports of its own aviation fuel as it attempts to preserve domestic supplies.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“To meet the needs of combat and civilian aviation, Russia, which for decades positioned itself as an energy superpower, has officially introduced a temporary ban on exports of its own aviation fuel and is forced to seek ways to import foreign Jet A-1 aviation fuel,” Ukrainian intelligence said.
Jet A-1 is broadly comparable to the Soviet- and Russian-standard TS-1 and RT kerosene fuels used in gas-turbine aircraft engines, allowing it to be used by a wide range of aircraft operated by the Russian military.
HUR said the imported fuel is suitable for aircraft including the MiG-29, Su-34, Su-35S, Su-30SM, Su-57 and Su-24M, as well as Tu-95MS strategic bombers.
The fuel could also be used by Russia’s newer jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones, which employ Telefly TJ2000A turbojet engines or Russian-made equivalents designated TRD-2000.
Ukrainian intelligence said three tankers linked to Russia’s shadow fleet have already delivered approximately 70,000 metric tons of Jet A-1 from South Korea and Egypt to Russian ports in St. Petersburg and Vladivostok.
The shipments were reportedly arranged for Russia’s Independent Oil and Gas Company, which supplies large quantities of fuel to TZK-AERO.
TZK-AERO, in turn, provides fuel under government contracts to the Russian military, the Federal Security Service and other Russian security formations, according to HUR.
Ukrainian intelligence said the supply chain for South Korean aviation fuel involved UAE-based Caliph Energy Trading FZE.
The Egyptian supply route reportedly involved the Middle East Oil Refinery, known as MIDOR, the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation and UAE-based trading company Vernal Overseas FZE.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia was considering easing aviation fuel standards in an effort to increase production following Ukrainian strikes on the country’s oil refineries.
Russia’s Transport Ministry has proposed allowing aviation fuel with a freezing point of up to minus 50 degrees Celsius, compared with the current requirement of minus 60 degrees Celsius.

articles.title: Iraq committed to full US withdrawal deadline – media
articles.body:
Iraq committed to full US withdrawal deadline – media
Iraq is committed to a full withdrawal of US-led coalition forces by the end of September, UK-based Saudi daily Asharq Al-Awsat reported on Saturday, citing an Iraqi official.
US forces have been in the country for 23 years since the 2003 invasion and subsequent smaller-scale operations against Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS).
Reports that US and other foreign troops could remain after September “contradict what was agreed upon between the previous Iraqi government and the US administration,” Asharq Al-Awsat cited the official as saying.
The comments followed media reports suggesting that Washington was only planning a drawdown, rather than a full withdraw by the end of the September deadline.
“This is a transition of the Coalition’s military mission to a more traditional bilateral security partnership,” Iraqi news outlet Shafaq News reported, citing an anonymous US official.
Earlier this month, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s office stated that the September 30 deadline would be “the fixed and final date” for the pullout of international coalition forces.
US President Donald Trump has previously backed reducing the US military presence in Iraq, reaffirming a withdrawal plan originally agreed in 2024 under the Biden administration. During a meeting with al-Zaidi this summer, Trump said the two countries were developing a relationship “where we don’t need the military” in Iraq.
Washington’s presence in the region has taken a significant hit during the Iran war, as Tehran has damaged or outright destroyed key US radar, communications, and other military infrastructure at bases in Gulf nations.
During the conflict, US military infrastructure in the region also faced attacks by pro-Iranian armed groups in Iraq operating outside Baghdad’s direct control.
The Pentagon is now considering whether to reduce the US military footprint in the Gulf after the Iran war ends, The Washington Post reported earlier in August, citing anonymous officials.
US allies in the Gulf have also reportedly expressed frustration over what they see as a lack of proper consultation before the US-Israeli attack on Iran, which led to bases on their territories being targeted. Regional powers have since moved to diversify their security partnerships, with Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan signing the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, already dubbed by commentators an ‘Islamic NATO,’ early this month.

articles.title: Ukrainian USF destroy five Russian air defense assets at Yeysk and Millerovo airfields
articles.body:
Ukrainian USF destroy five Russian air defense assets at Yeysk and Millerovo airfields
According to Ukrinform, Robert “Madyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, reported this on Facebook.
According to Brovdi, during the August 30 operation against Russian military airfields, drones operated by the “Birds” of the First Separate Center struck a Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft missile and gun system, a Sopka-2 (12L6) radar station and an aviation weapons depot in Yeysk, Krasnodar Krai.
In Shabelskoye, Krasnodar Krai, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck a Kasta 2E2 radar station.
At the Millerovo airfield, located near the settlement of Dolotinka in Russia’s Rostov region, ammunition depots and a technical and maintenance unit were destroyed.
The forces also struck an RSP-27 (DRL-27) radar and a Nebo-SV radar in Dolotinka.
According to Madyar, the main target of the operation was the DRL-27 module of the RSP-27 aircraft landing radar system at the Millerovo airfield. The destroyed DRL-27 is an airfield control radar that, in addition to detecting airborne targets, is an integral component of air traffic control and operates as part of a system with the PRL-27 landing radar.
“The destruction of the above-mentioned enemy air defense assets has been confirmed by additional reconnaissance,” the USF commander said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine’s Defense Forces previously struck a Russian radar station, command posts and a Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft missile and gun system.

articles.title: Putin, Xi set for Central Asia summit as Russia and China seek to counter Western influence
articles.body:
Putin, Xi set for Central Asia summit as Russia and China seek to counter Western influence
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping are due in Kyrgyzstan on Monday for a two-day summit, joined by the leaders of Iran and India. The gathering comes as the group seeks to project a united front amid wars in Ukraine and Iran and growing tensions with the West.
Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping are expected in Central Asia's Kyrgyzstan Monday for a two-day summit, also attended by Iran's and India's leaders, of a regional bloc seeking to be a counter-influence to the West.
Around a dozen heads of states will head to the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek to mark 25 years of the Shanghai Cooperation Group (SCO).
The group brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West.
It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow's Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran. Iran will be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian.
Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as India's Narendra Modi and Pakistan's Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz leader Sadyr Japarov.
Read moreXi hosts Putin and Modi at SCO summit in show of Global South unity
Putin is also expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Iran's Pezeshkian and China's Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said.
Russia and Iran – among the most sanctioned states in the world – have massively deepened their military and economic ties during the Ukraine war.
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran.
Putin's meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA's director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues. It gained momentum in recent years under Moscow's and Beijing's leadership.
On top of its 10 members, it now has 15 "dialogue partners", including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.
The SCO's founding declaration says the group is "not an alliance directed against other states".
Read morePutin seeks to reinforce China ties after Trump-Xi summit
But Putin and Xi have repeatedly made anti-Western speeches during its summits.
At last year's gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced "acts of intimidation", referring to US-Chinese tensions.
Real and trade wars
The Bishkek summit takes place as some SCO members are in the midst of real wars – the Ukraine and Iran conflicts – or trade wars, with the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Indian goods.
This month, the US slapped secondary sanctions on Iran's trading partners in the sectors of gold, technology, digital assets, aviation, and maritime transport, aiming to cripple the Iranian regime.
Washington also threatened Iran's allies with sanctions.
China, a major importer of Iranian oil, responded by saying it will "firmly defend" its interests.
Iran, living under sanctions since its 1979 revolution ended with Islamic authorities taking charge, has regularly said it will not cave to economic pressure.
But Pezeshkian has acknowledged his country faces "economic difficulties".
Iran only joined the bloc in 2023.
Read moreChina summit a symbol of a world aiming to 'make itself America-proof', expert says
Mohammad Hassan Najmi, an international relations expert, told AFP that Tehran "believes its membership and active participation in these alliances can enable it to circumvent US and European sanctions".

articles.title: US military leaders warn Hegseth over 'unsustainable' Iran war duration: report
articles.body:
Senior US military commanders have warned Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that the continuing war against Iran is “unsustainable” and threatens the country’s ability to respond to global crises and defend the homeland, The Washington Post reported.
The warnings appeared in the August 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book, a classified internal document used to direct military movements.
People familiar with the assessment said the latest edition requires certain personnel currently in the Middle East to remain there through September, while other units have been ordered to continue their deployments into 2027.
The heads of the army, navy and air force, along with four-star commanders responsible for operations in Europe, Asia and Latin America, characterised the six-month war as “too much for too long”.
The leaders of US European Command, US Indo-Pacific Command and US Southern Command, as well as the Navy’s top admiral, formally registered their “non-concurrence” with orders extending the deployment of their forces in the Middle East.
Although the move signals formal disagreement with the defence secretary’s directive, the commanders confirmed that they would still carry out the mission.
The report said the reassignment of ships and surveillance aircraft to US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, had reduced the military’s capacity for training and homeland defence.
The navy has reportedly stretched its resources to meet wartime demands, raising concerns that insufficient ship maintenance could result in fleet shortages if other conflicts emerge.
Although the Army and Air Force leadership formally concurred with the deployment extensions, they warned that the decision carried “significant risk”.
More than 50,000 US troops are currently stationed in the region.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell declined to discuss the orders book or specific internal disagreements.
He said force allocation decisions were based on “strategic priorities established by the president and the advice of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and Combatant Commanders”.
It remains unclear when the overstretched units will be allowed to return to their original areas of operation.

31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026

articles.title: Putin-Trump-Zelensky summit possible only to 'formalize agreements,' Peskov says
articles.body:
A summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump, and President Volodymyr Zelensky could take place only to formalize agreements already reached, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Aug. 30, according to Russian state-controlled media.
The comments come as peace efforts remain stalled, with Russia continuing to insist on its maximalist conditions and attacking Ukrainian cities.
"Such a meeting is possible only to formalize agreements," Peskov told reporters. He added that a settlement over Ukraine is "not a primitive deal," but a "very complicated" process involving "a huge number of details."
The latest statement follows a recent visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe. Peskov said Ratcliffe met with Russian intelligence officials but did not meet Putin, who was briefed on the discussions. Trump described the Aug. 25 visit as "semi-routine."
Russia has repeatedly rejected or complicated proposals aimed at advancing ceasefire talks. On Aug. 22, Putin said Moscow said he received new proposals for ending the war, calling them "exotic" and "unacceptable."
"The proposals being conveyed to us are sometimes, I would say, exotic in nature and are unacceptable," Putin said. He added that Russia was ready for peace talks only "on the basis of the realities that have developed on the ground," a position he has reiterated throughout the past few years.
The Kremlin has also rejected proposals for a partial aerial ceasefire, while U.S. and Ukrainian officials have explored new approaches to move negotiations forward. Moscow has also rejected other proposals, including an American suggestion to establish a free economic zone in Donbas.

articles.title: Israel pounds southern Lebanon as Iran vows to stand by Beirut

Israel pounds southern Lebanon as Iran vows to stand by Beirut
Israel continued attacks across southern Lebanon on Saturday, carrying out airstrikes, artillery shelling and demolitions, while Tehran pledged continued support for the country amid stalled negotiations over an IDF withdrawal.
Most of the day’s attacks were concentrated in Nabatieh Province, RT’s Lebanon correspondent Steve Sweeney said. Two explosions were reported near Aita al-Jabal, while Israeli drones carried out two strikes on Nabatieh al-Fawqa on Saturday morning. Israeli forces separately set fire to homes in Beit Yahoun.
The latest strikes came two days after an Israeli attack on Arab Salim killed 28-year-old Saja Sharara just 48 hours after her wedding, according to Sweeney, who recently visited the southern Lebanese village. Six others were wounded, including a child, a woman, and two elderly people.
Israel, however, said Thursday’s strikes followed the launch of two Hezbollah drones toward Israeli troops.
The escalation comes as Tehran reaffirms its support for Lebanon. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Sheikh Ali al-Khatib, vice president of Lebanon’s Higher Shiite Islamic Council, in Tehran on Friday. According to Lebanese L’Orient Today, Khatib described a deteriorating situation in the south, saying many displaced residents had exhausted their savings and had been left without homes or work. He appealed in particular for financial assistance for affected communities.
Araghchi said Tehran was working to revive the US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed in June, the first clause of which called for an end to Israeli attacks on Lebanon. He argued that implementing the agreement remained the way to resolve the crisis, while acknowledging that “the circumstances are difficult,” as cited by L’Orient Today.
The memorandum followed a renewed escalation between Israel and Hezbollah after the latter resumed attacks two days after the US-Iran war began on February 28. Hezbollah said its operation was retaliation for the killing of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
Hezbollah says it has observed the ceasefire reached under the subsequent US-Iran agreement. Israel, however, has continued strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon and currently occupies more than 600 square kilometers of Lebanese territory.
Beirut and Israel have meanwhile been holding direct negotiations aimed at securing an Israeli withdrawal and ending the hostilities. Another round is reportedly expected in Rome in September, but progress has been limited.

articles.title: US military chiefs warn Hegseth that Iran war is weakening forces needed to counter intl. threats

The heads of the US armed forces jointly warned US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth against continuing operations in Iran, The Washington Post reported on Sunday.
According to people familiar with the matter, the heads of the army, navy, and air force, along with the commanders who head the US military’s operations in Europe, Asia, and Latin America, warned Hegseth that continuing the war in Iran risks weakening their ability to confront threats elsewhere around the world.
The warnings were detailed in the August 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book (SDOB), which is classified. The people with knowledge spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The SDOB details the worldwide availability of the US’s military assets, such as warships, aircraft, personnel, and weapons systems. It also reflects the president’s priorities for the armed forces, which the defense secretary and the branches of the military carry out.
US military heads disagree with Hegseth orders to keep troops in Middle East until 2027, still will carry it out
The orders book reportedly stated some US troops deployed in the Middle East to remain there through September, while others would remain in the region until 2027, sources familiar with the matter said.
The Washington Post reported that the navy’s top admiral, along with the leaders from America’s European Command, Pacific Command, and the Southern Command, responded with “non-concur,” which means that they do not agree with Hegseth’s order, but will execute it regardless.
Leaders from the US Army and Air Force both noted that the extension of their forces comes with significant risks.
One person familiar with the matter said that US military leadership believes that the war in Iran has been “too much for too long.”
“Decisions regarding the scope and duration of specific force commitments to any Combatant Command are made based on the current threat assessment, strategic priorities established by the President, and the advice of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and Combatant Commanders,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to the Washington Post.
He added that the Pentagon “does not discuss internal operational processes,” such as the SDOB, “or specific concurrences, non-concurrences, or risk assessments provided by the Services or Combatant Commands during force allocation deliberations.”

articles.title: U.S. Army’s newest tank prototype heads to 1st Cavalry Division
articles.body:
- The U.S. Army's 1st Cavalry Division will test M1E3 Abrams and XM30 prototypes, according to the division's own social media announcement.
- The M1E3 is designed with a hybrid-electric drive, an autoloader and integrated protection in a lighter frame than current Abrams tanks.
The U.S. Army will send its M1E3 Abrams prototype to the 1st Cavalry Division for testing, the division confirmed in a social media post responding to an Army announcement about the next-generation tank.
The 1st Cavalry Division said it will receive both M1E3 prototypes and XM30 prototypes, testing the vehicles and providing feedback that will help shape the Army’s approach to future armored formations.
“And guess who gets to play with them first. The First Team will receive not only the M1E3 prototypes but also the XM30 prototypes to test, provide feedback on and to shape the future of Armored warfare,” the division wrote.
The Army’s announcement described the M1E3 as featuring a hybrid-electric drive, an autoloader and integrated protection systems built into a lighter frame than the current Abrams variants in service.
“The M1E3 Abrams represents a bold step forward in modern vehicle design, combining advanced protection, reduced weight, and a smaller logistical footprint to meet the challenges of tomorrow’s battlefield,” said Michelle Link, Deputy Capability Program Executive for Ground Combat Platforms.
The Army first showed the M1E3 publicly on January 14 at the Detroit Auto Show, presenting it as an early demonstrator built to test unmanned turret architecture, crew layout, digital systems and automation ahead of a planned M1A3 production tank. The design followed the Army’s earlier AbramsX concept demonstrator and reflects lessons the service says it drew from combat losses of donor Abrams tanks in Ukraine, where independent trackers and Ukrainian officials have reported significant losses among the 31 M1A1 tanks delivered, with estimates varying by source.
The most significant change from earlier Abrams variants is the unmanned turret. All three crew members, the commander, gunner and driver, are relocated into an armored crew capsule in the forward hull rather than sitting inside the turret itself, removing them from the tank’s most exposed section.
For targeting, the M1E3 uses the Leonardo DRS Stabilized Sight System, known as S3, as the commander’s panoramic sight, replacing the Safran PASEO system used on the earlier AbramsX demonstrator. The S3 is available in long-wave and mid-wave infrared variants and is also used on the Army’s M-LIDS counter-drone system.
Secondary armament comes from an EOS R400 Mk2 remote weapon station mounted atop the turret. In its displayed configuration, the station combines a 40mm Mk19 automatic grenade launcher, a 7.62mm machine gun and a launcher holding a single FGM-148 Javelin anti-tank missile. The R400 Mk2 is paired with an EchoGuard radar system for detecting and tracking small drones, giving the tank a built-in counter-UAS capability. Army representatives have said the weapon station’s loadout is modular and can be reconfigured depending on mission needs.
The Army has described the overall approach as built around a Modular Open Systems Architecture, intended to let new sensors, weapons and electronic warfare systems be added later through standardized interfaces rather than requiring a full redesign.
The Army has said four early M1E3 prototypes are planned, intended for testing with operational units to evaluate how the new features perform in practice, with serial production targeted for the end of the decade.
Separately, the XM30 program aims to replace the Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle, with General Dynamics Land Systems and American Rheinmetall Vehicles competing as finalists. General Dynamics delivered its XM30 Wolf prototype to the Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground last week.
The Army has not disclosed a specific delivery date for the M1E3 prototypes to the 1st Cavalry Division, based at Fort Cavazos, Texas, the total number of prototypes involved in this testing phase, or a timeline for when soldier feedback will inform further development of the design.

articles.title: Ukraine offers invaluable lessons to NATO, from new technologies to national resilience – expert
articles.body:
Ukraine offers invaluable lessons to NATO, from new technologies to national resilience – expert
Can Kasapoğlu, Senior Fellow and Defense Analyst at Hudson Institute, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Ukraine offers invaluable lessons to NATO. The first one is pennies versus dollars. Affordable, scalable, sustainable mass can outperform exquisite systems in combat,” Kasapoğlu said.
According to the expert, comparing the cost of Ukrainian drones with the value of the Russian equipment they destroy showed how defense-economics asymmetry can systematically impose attrition.
In his view, the second important lesson is the need to assess “red lines” rather than mythologize them.
“Ukraine sank the Moskva, struck Moscow, attacked Crimea and Alabuga, damaged energy infrastructure, and hit strategic-bomber bases through Operation Spiderweb. Before the war, Western analyses portrayed such actions as possible thresholds for Russian tactical nuclear use. That escalation did not occur. The risk remains, but deterrence requires empirical judgment, not paralysis,” Kasapoğlu said.
The expert identified national resilience as the third lesson.
“Few expected Ukraine to withstand a war of this scale, making national resilience-building as important as weapons procurement,” he stressed.
In addition, Kasapoğlu said, NATO must prepare for protracted interstate wars.
As reported by Ukrinform, peace requires pressure on every member of the coalition supporting Russia until continuing the war forces them into a serious dilemma and a settlement begins to offer them benefits.

articles.title: Russia attacks Ukraine with two Iskander missiles and 130 drones overnight
articles.body:
Russia attacks Ukraine with two Iskander missiles and 130 drones overnight
Russia attacked Ukraine with two Iskander-M ballistic missiles and 130 drones of various types on the night of 29-30 August. Hits were recorded at 13 locations.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: Russian forces launched two Iskander-M ballistic missiles from Russia's Kursk Oblast and 130 Shahed and Gerbera loitering munitions, S8000 Banderol drone missiles and Parodiya decoy drones. Most of the drones were jet-powered.
Early reports indicate that Ukrainian air defences shot down or jammed 125 Russian drones.
The Air Force recorded hits by Russian weapons at 13 locations, and debris from downed assets landed at four locations.
In addition, some Russian assets failed to reach their targets, and information about them is being confirmed.
The attack was still ongoing at the time of publication.

articles.title: PLA shift to systems warfare means Taiwan’s defences need to change: experts
articles.body:
PLA shift to systems warfare means Taiwan’s defences need to change: experts
Conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have shown the power of integration and the extension of targets to include critical civilian infrastructure
Instead of focusing on individual weapons, the PLA has progressively emphasised integrating intelligence, AI, communications, weapons, logistics and infrastructure into an overall combat system, they warn.
“The PLA is no longer concerned only with whose weapons are stronger, but with who can connect different weapons to generate greater overall combat power,” said Chen Chia-sheng, a researcher at a government-funded think tank in Taipei.
In an article published last week by his organisation, the Institute for National Defence and Security Research, Chen wrote that for Taiwan, this meant the threat in a cross-strait conflict could extend well beyond attacks on its fighters, warships and missile batteries.
Under what the PLA calls “systems destruction warfare”, Beijing could seek to disable critical nodes supporting Taiwanese forces, including satellites, radar, communications links, command centres, data networks and fuel and logistics facilities, he wrote.
Once those links were severed, even sophisticated weapons could rapidly lose their effectiveness without being physically destroyed, he added.

articles.title: In the autumn, the rate of downing Russian drones must be brought above 90% — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
In the autumn, the rate of downing Russian drones must be brought above 90% — Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
Over four days, Russia launched nearly 1,500 drones, around 800 of them jet-powered. Ukraine is strengthening its air defense and developing interceptor drones.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on the Ministry of Defense and the military to maximize efforts to strengthen capabilities to counter Russian drones, so that by autumn the rate of their destruction exceeds 90%. The head of state reported this on Telegram, UNN writes.
Today, our military reported on the protection of the skies. Russia’s current tactic is to exhaust Ukraine, to exhaust Ukrainians, primarily our people
According to him, Russian troops are constantly attacking Ukraine with drones, in particular using many jet-powered "Shaheds." Ukrainian military personnel shoot down a significant proportion of the drones.
There were almost 1,500 drones of all types in just these four days, of which about 800 were jet-powered
Zelenskyy noted that the most difficult task is destroying the jet-powered drones specifically. Currently, the main means of protection against them is combat aviation.
He reported that Ukraine is working to obtain the necessary interceptor drones. According to the President, four companies have already developed the relevant unmanned aircraft, with one of them having the most successful equipment.
Right now, the Ministry of Defense and the military alike—everyone must do their utmost to ensure that we have the greatest possible capabilities to shoot down each type of Russian drone
The President thanked all members of Ukraine’s team who are working around the clock to strengthen the protection of the skies.
In the autumn, we need to respond and ensure that the destruction rate is definitely above 90%

articles.title: Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella says soldiers killed key dissident leader
articles.body:
Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella says soldiers killed key dissident leader
Operations against illegal armed groups will continue, the president said, and criminals who do not surrender will ‘end up in a body bag’
A prominent leader of the dissident factions of the defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia who operated in a volatile area in the country’s southwest region was killed on Sunday during a military operation, said President Abelardo de la Espriella.
The president said the death of a man known as “Felipe” or “Arcadio” was a “crushing blow” to the dissident faction led by a man who goes by “Ivan Mordisco”.
De la Espriella posted a video on social media presumably showing a person in a body bag near a weapon and ammunition seized by authorities during the operation.
“We are closing the net on Mordisco and his networks,” warned the president, who announced that offensive operations against illegal armed groups would continue. “Any criminal who doesn’t surrender will end up in a body bag.”
He said “Felipe” was responsible for multiple attacks on police stations in Valle del Cauca, using explosives dropped from drones. He commanded a unit within the Jaime Martinez faction, part of the dissident groups of the defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) that refused to join the government’s 2016 peace negotiations.
The leader also took part in planting explosives-laden gas cylinders on roads in Valle del Cauca, attacking a military unit, torching cars, engaging in extortion and committing other criminal acts, de la Espriella said.

articles.title: Russia is preparing to return a missile cruiser to service after nearly 30 years of repairs
articles.body:
Russia is preparing to return a missile cruiser to service after nearly 30 years of repairs
Kyiv • UNN
The nuclear-powered cruiser “Admiral Nakhimov” is completing trials after modernization. The ship will receive 80 missile launchers and cost more than 200 billion rubles.
Russia expects to return the nuclear-powered missile cruiser "Admiral Nakhimov," which has been undergoing repairs and modernization for nearly 30 years, to the fleet's active service. The ship is currently completing its shipyard and sea trials, Defense Express reports, according to UNN.
Details
By the end of the year, the Russians plan to conduct state trials of the ship, after which it could theoretically return to the Russian Navy.
In fact, the "Admiral Nakhimov" arrived for repairs as early as July 1997, although it was officially placed under repair in August 1999. The cruiser entered service in 1988.
The cruiser can carry up to 80 missiles
After modernization, the ship is to receive 80 launchers for Kalibr, Oniks, and Tsirkon missiles, which would make it one of the most heavily armed ships in the Russian fleet.
According to Russian estimates, the repairs and modernization have already cost more than 200 billion rubles, or approximately $2.3 billion. At the same time, the project's cost was previously estimated at roughly $5 billion.
Defense Express notes that the advisability of such expenditure on a single large ship raises questions, particularly due to the development of naval drones and other means of destruction that increase the vulnerability of large surface platforms.

articles.title: Ankara summons Ukraine envoy after Black Sea attacks
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone strikes a Turkish-owned roll-on/roll-off (ro-ro) cargo ship near Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk earlier this month.
Türkiye summoned Ukraine’s ambassador on Aug. 29 after two Turkish-operated commercial vessels were damaged in separate drone attacks in the Black Sea near the Russian port of Tuapse, according to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources.
Ukrainian Ambassador Naryman Dzhelialov was called to the Foreign Ministry in Ankara after the attacks on the Lider Bordo Mavi and Lider Kocatepe vessels, the sources said.
The Lider Bordo Mavi was struck Aug. 26 while sailing near Tuapse, according to Turkish shipping and regional sources. The vessel, which was carrying fresh produce, caught fire after being hit by three drones, injuring five crew members.
The ship flies the Cameroon flag and is operated by a Turkish company. It had departed from the Turkish Black Sea port of Samsun around Aug. 25 and was headed for Tuapse after reportedly being unable to call at the Russian port of Novorossiysk.
The Lider Kocatepe was sent to the area the following day to assist the damaged vessel but was itself targeted by a drone while en route, according to media reports. It sustained material damage and returned to Samsun.
Ukraine did not immediately publicly claim responsibility for either attack. Russia has attributed similar recent strikes on commercial shipping to Ukrainian forces.
The incidents have heightened concerns over the safety of commercial vessels operating in the Black Sea, where civilian shipping has increasingly been exposed to the effects of the war between Russia and Ukraine.
During the meeting, Turkish officials conveyed Ankara’s concerns over the attacks and stressed the need to protect lives, property, navigation and the marine environment, the ministry sources said.
Türkiye has repeatedly warned that the war should not further threaten civilian maritime traffic or disrupt commercial navigation in the Black Sea. Türkiye has sought to maintain relations with both Russia and Ukraine while positioning itself as a mediator in efforts to limit the war’s impact on civilian and commercial activity.
The full extent of the damage to both vessels was still being assessed on Aug. 31.

articles.title: Chinese fighter jet based on Israeli design sold to Muslim-majority Uzbekistan
articles.body:
Another Muslim country is receiving the legacy of a previous Israeli aircraft project as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructs the defense establishment to prepare for the development of a new Israeli fighter jet in an effort to maintain Israel’s defense independence.
A video broadcast on Uzbek television confirmed that Uzbekistan will become the second customer of China’s J-10C fighter jet, after Pakistan became the first country to purchase the aircraft.
The J-10 bears a strong resemblance to Israel’s Lavi fighter jet, developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), whose production was canceled after a government decision in 1988.
According to foreign reports, China later bought the Lavi's plans to accelerate the development of a domestically produced fourth-generation fighter jet and modernize its air force. The funds China paid helped cover the costs of ending the project in Israel.
The Chinese fighter has already been used in combat, participating in aerial clashes between Pakistan and India last year. The aircraft was reportedly used to shoot down Indian Air Force Rafale fighter jets while carrying the advanced PL-15 radar-guided missile.
Uzbekistan's order reflects increasing Chinese influence in Central Asia
Uzbekistan has ordered 24 J-10 aircraft in the export configuration, a move that reflects China’s growing influence in Central Asia, where countries were previously under Russian influence.
The aircraft, which originated in Lod, is now serving a second Muslim country, although one that maintains diplomatic relations with Israel.
According to assessments, Muslim-majority Bangladesh could also become the next customer for the J-10. The aircraft is cheaper than the American F-16 and is marketed to countries that are not interested in purchasing US-made fighter jets.

articles.title: Ukraine develops stationary EW and SIGINT system for detecting and jamming FPV drones
articles.body:
Ukraine develops stationary EW and SIGINT system for detecting and jamming FPV drones
Ukrainian defence company Rebel Group has developed a stationary electronic warfare and signals intelligence system called Brama. The company plans to have it codified for use by Ukraine's Defence Forces.
Source: Rebel Group press service
Details: The system combines electronic warfare and signals intelligence functions and is designed to counter FPV drones.
"The system can detect the frequency of analogue video and decode it, and then jam both the video channel and the drone's control channel using directed electronic warfare," the press service said.
When the Brama operator receives data on a target and detects it, they can immediately jam it without any additional equipment. Rebel Group also said that the system has undergone range and laboratory testing.
The Ukrainian company is undergoing the codification procedure in order to have the system approved for use by the defence forces.
Rebel Group is a technology company specialising in development and production of electronic warfare and signals intelligence systems. Some of its systems have been codified and tested at General Staff ranges.
Background:
- Ukrainian company InLab previously presented the Stryi electronic warfare station, designed to counter FPV drones and other unmanned aerial vehicles.
- Defence company Unwave also conducted its first testing of its own electronic warfare systems abroad, showcasing the systems in Czechia.

articles.title: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | Letters
articles.body:
Timothy Garton Ash is right that serious artificial intelligence risks demand international action, but “AI Hiroshima” may be the wrong picture (Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not, 22 August). Hiroshima was not technology going rogue. Human beings designed the bomb, authorised its use and dropped it. The technology worked much as intended.
AI may one day behave in ways we cannot control, but many of the gravest harms could happen without any dramatic moment when “the AI takes over”. AI might help design a pathogen, find a vulnerability in critical infrastructure or improve a weapons system while people still decide what happens next. Other harms may build almost invisibly through thousands of ordinary decisions – more autonomy here, one safeguard removed there, another consequential task handed over because the system has worked well so far. By the time the danger is obvious, the important decisions may already have been made.
That is also where international agreement could begin. We do not need countries to agree about superintelligence or the probability of human extinction before agreeing that there are some doors AI should never be allowed to open by itself. Weapons systems, critical infrastructure and biological synthesis are obvious places to start. Governments could agree minimum safeguards, require clear human authority for the most consequential actions, keep records of who authorised what and share serious failures and near-misses internationally.
The greatest AI dangers may not arrive with a mushroom cloud. They may arrive quietly, one apparently reasonable step at a time. If we want effective AI governance, we need to fight the right battle, not the most cinematic one.
Dr Simon Nieder
Chesterfield, Derbyshire
Prof Jonathan Michie (Letters, 26 August) reminds us that the Serbelloni group, led by the author’s father, Donald Michie (when he was at Edinburgh University), was weighing the social dangers of artificial intelligence as long ago as 1972. Nor is AI technology itself new, since its roots run back through to Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron of 1957, to the Dartmouth workshop of 1956, and to Alan Turing before that. What is new is that we now have the hardware and software infrastructures to drive it forward at what can sometimes seem to be a terrifying speed.
The Lighthill report of 1973 duly delivered an AI winter in the UK, and the field’s centre of gravity crossed the Atlantic, with the consequences that we all now live with. Donald Michie had worked alongside Turing at Bletchley Park and argued forcefully against the cuts, in the televised Lighthill debate that followed the report, to no avail. The quip attributed to him, perhaps apocryphally, “Let there be Lighthill. And there was darkness”, still resonates strongly in our country today.
As a double-hatted academic (computer scientist and humanities scholar), I would argue for the return of a “Serbelloni debate” that, as Jonathan Michie observes and as his father recognised, requires the involvement of both the sciences and the humanities.
Dr Anthony Harris
Emmanuel College, Cambridge
In his article about regulating AI (I worked at OpenAI. Here are the guardrails we need now, 21 August), Miles Brundage failed to mention an international effort seeking broad political support for a global AI treaty. This effort is carrying forward a compelling address at the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva last month, where the secretary general called for human control of AI as its applications spread in weaponry and subversive, prejudicial public surveillance
A fragmented approach, as described by Mr Brundage, is likely to greatly increase the difficulty of implementing AI controls that are timely, internationally negotiated, and therefore effective.
AI, corporate agendas, diverse national defence and economic goals, and the proliferation of energy-intensive datacentres are entangled in interlocking systemic interrelationships that cannot be resolved through disjointed incrementalism. This is especially true as the pace of innovation accelerates, exacerbating worst-case scenarios of advanced AI technology, posing increasingly dire risks.
No matter how well intended, fragmented efforts will be diversionary and cause crucial delays, impeding the diligent pursuit of a systemic global strategy to pre-empt destructive outcomes. Such outcomes could result from malicious use of AI by humans and/or subversive and deceptive activities of renegade algorithms – examples of which are already alarming.
Another troubling aspect of this systemic dilemma must be addressed. Mounting bipartisan opposition to datacentres – well-justified and well-substantiated – is diverting the political attention needed to control AI and implement appropriate restraints (bans or moratoriums) until reliable AI safeguards can be established. This is analogous to focusing on treating a serious symptom in lieu of urgently seeking a remedy for the critical disease that’s causing it. Surely it’s possible to employ a multifaceted strategy, recognising that the sooner rigorous AI guardrails are established, the fewer datacentre harms will be suffered.
Like climate change, the threats of advanced AI are inherently global, making an international approach essential.
David Kyler
Saint Simons Island, Georgia, US
